lessons.title: 1.1 Introduction to Physics and Its Branches
lessons.notes_html:
Physics is the branch of science that studies matter, energy and their interaction. It observes nature, represents it mathematically and concludes with experiment. The word 'physics' comes from the ancient Greek word 'physicos', meaning knowledge of nature.

Branches of Physics

  • Mechanics — motion of objects (e.g. riding a bicycle).
  • Thermodynamics — heat and energy (e.g. cooking a barbecue).
  • Electricity — electric charges and circuits (e.g. turning a bulb on).
  • Astrophysics — stars, galaxies and the universe (e.g. looking for giant galaxies).
  • Acoustics — sound (e.g. producing a loud sound).
  • Atomic Physics — the structure of the atom (e.g. describing an atom).
  • Geophysics — the Earth and energy obtained from it.

Why Study Physics?

Physicists are categorised into two groups: those who do experiments from home to large-scale experiment labs, and those who work on theories. Physics lies in the laws that govern the whole universe, from an atom to large-scale galaxies.

mcqs.q: Cooking a barbecue belongs to which branch of physics?
mcqs.why: Cooking involves heat and energy transfer, which is the subject of thermodynamics. Mechanics deals with motion, acoustics with sound, and geophysics with the Earth.

mcqs.q: Riding a bicycle is an example studied in which branch of physics?
mcqs.why: Riding a bicycle is about the motion of an object, so it belongs to mechanics, the branch of physics that studies motion and forces.

mcqs.q: Looking for giant galaxies belongs to which branch of physics?
mcqs.why: Galaxies are huge objects in the universe. Their study is astrophysics, the branch dealing with stars, galaxies and the universe.

mcqs.q: Producing a loud sound belongs to which branch of physics?
mcqs.why: Sound is studied in acoustics. Producing and hearing a loud sound is a sound phenomenon, so it belongs to the acoustics branch.

mcqs.q: Turning a bulb on belongs to which branch of physics?
mcqs.why: A bulb lights up when electric current passes through it, so switching it on belongs to electricity, the branch about charges and circuits.

mcqs.q: Describing an atom belongs to which branch of physics?
mcqs.why: The atom and its internal structure are studied in atomic physics. Astrophysics, despite the similar name, deals with very large objects like galaxies.

mcqs.q: Obtaining energy from the Earth belongs to which branch of physics?
mcqs.why: Energy drawn from the Earth (such as geothermal energy) is studied in geophysics, the branch of physics concerned with the Earth.

mcqs.q: The word 'physics' is derived from the Greek word 'physicos', which means:
mcqs.why: Physics is derived from the ancient Greek word 'physicos', meaning 'knowledge of nature', because physics studies the natural world around us.

mcqs.q: Physics can be defined as the branch of science which observes nature and concludes with:
mcqs.why: Physics observes nature, represents it mathematically and finally concludes with experiment. A conclusion in physics must be confirmed by experiment.

mcqs.q: Physicists are categorised into two categories: those who perform experiments and those who:
mcqs.why: Physicists fall into two categories: experimental physicists, who perform experiments from home to large-scale labs, and theoretical physicists, who work on theories.

lessons.title: Physical Quantities and the International System of Units (SI)
lessons.notes_html:
A physical quantity is anything that can be measured, e.g. length, mass and time. Quantities whose units are fixed by definition are base quantities; quantities obtained by combining base quantities are derived quantities.

Base Quantities and Their SI Units

  • Length — metre (m)
  • Mass — kilogram (kg)
  • Time — second (s)
  • Electric current — ampere (A)
  • Temperature — kelvin (K)
  • Amount of substance — mole (mol)
  • Luminous intensity — candela (cd)

Derived Quantities (examples)

  • Volume — m³ (derived)
  • Force — newton (N) (derived)
  • Density — kg m&sup-3; (derived)
  • Acceleration — m s&sup-2; (derived)

The worldwide system in which the units of the base quantities were set up is called the International System of Units (SI).

mcqs.q: The worldwide measurement system in which the units of the base quantities were set up is called:
mcqs.why: The SI (International System of Units) is the worldwide system that fixes the units of the base quantities, such as the metre, kilogram and second.

mcqs.q: Length, mass, electric current, time, luminous intensity and amount of substance are examples of:
mcqs.why: These quantities are measured directly with their own fixed units, so they are base quantities. Derived quantities, like force and volume, are built from them.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of electric current is:
mcqs.why: Electric current is a base quantity and its SI unit is the ampere (A). Kelvin is for temperature, mole for amount of substance and candela for luminous intensity.

mcqs.q: A quantity whose unit is m³ is:
mcqs.why: Volume is measured in cubic metres (m³). It is a derived quantity because it is obtained by multiplying three lengths together.

mcqs.q: The unit newton (N) belongs to which quantity, and of which type?
mcqs.why: The newton is the unit of force. Force is a derived quantity because its unit is built from base units: 1 N = 1 kg m s&sup-2;.

mcqs.q: Temperature is a base quantity. Its SI unit is:
mcqs.why: In the SI system temperature is measured in kelvin (K). Celsius and Fahrenheit are common scales, but kelvin is the SI base unit.

mcqs.q: Density has the SI unit kg m&sup-3;. Density is:
mcqs.why: Density = mass / volume, so its unit kg m&sup-3; is built from the base units kg and m. Any quantity made from base quantities is a derived quantity.

mcqs.q: Acceleration, with unit m s&sup-2;, is classified as:
mcqs.why: Acceleration = change of velocity / time, so its unit m s&sup-2; comes from base units. It is therefore a derived quantity.

mcqs.q: Time is a base quantity with SI unit:
mcqs.why: The SI base unit of time is the second (s). Minutes, hours and milliseconds are multiples or sub-multiples of the second, not the base unit.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a derived quantity?
mcqs.why: Force is derived because its unit, the newton, is a combination of base units (kg m s&sup-2;). Mass, length and time are base quantities.

lessons.title: Prefixes and Conversion of Units
lessons.notes_html:
Prefixes are used with SI units to show multiples and sub-multiples, e.g. kilo (10³), centi (10&sup-2;), milli (10&sup-3;), micro (10&sup-6;) and giga (10&sup9;).

Worked Conversions (from the book)

230 cm = 2.3 m

250 g = 0.25 kg

0.5 s = 500 ms

0.8 m = 800 mm

350 ms = 0.35 s

1.2 kg = 1200 g

Prefix Forms

  • 75 000 m = 750 hm (hectometre), since 750 × 100 m = 75 000 m
  • 1/1000 s = 1 ms (millisecond)
  • 1/1 000 000 g = 1 µg (microgram)
  • 1 000 000 000 m = 1 Gm (gigametre)

mcqs.q: 230 cm is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: 100 cm = 1 m. Step 2: 230 cm = 230 / 100 m = 2.3 m. To convert cm into m, divide by 100.

mcqs.q: 250 g is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: 1000 g = 1 kg. Step 2: 250 g = 250 / 1000 kg = 0.25 kg. To convert grams into kilograms, divide by 1000.

mcqs.q: 0.5 s is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: 1 s = 1000 ms. Step 2: 0.5 s = 0.5 × 1000 ms = 500 ms. Seconds are converted to milliseconds by multiplying by 1000.

mcqs.q: 0.8 m is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: 1 m = 1000 mm. Step 2: 0.8 m = 0.8 × 1000 mm = 800 mm. To convert metres into millimetres, multiply by 1000.

mcqs.q: 350 ms is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: 1000 ms = 1 s. Step 2: 350 ms = 350 / 1000 s = 0.35 s. Milliseconds are converted to seconds by dividing by 1000.

mcqs.q: 1.2 kg is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: 1 kg = 1000 g. Step 2: 1.2 kg = 1.2 × 1000 g = 1200 g. To convert kilograms into grams, multiply by 1000.

mcqs.q: 75 000 m written with a prefix is 750 ______:
mcqs.why: The hectometre (hm) is 100 m. Step: 750 × 100 m = 75 000 m, so 75 000 m = 750 hm. A kilometre would give 75 km instead.

mcqs.q: 1/1000 of a second is written as:
mcqs.why: Milli means one-thousandth (10&sup-3;), so 1/1000 s = 1 ms (millisecond). Micro is one-millionth and nano is one-billionth.

mcqs.q: 1/1 000 000 of a gram is:
mcqs.why: Micro means one-millionth (10&sup-6;), so one-millionth of a gram is 1 microgram (µg). A milligram is only one-thousandth of a gram.

mcqs.q: 1 000 000 000 m is equal to:
mcqs.why: Giga means 10&sup9; (one billion), so 1 000 000 000 m = 1 Gm (gigametre). Mega is only 10&sup6; and tera is 10¹².

lessons.title: Scientific Notation and Significant Figures
lessons.notes_html:
Scientific notation writes a number as a digit part between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10.

Examples (from the book)

  • Radius of the first orbit of the hydrogen atom: 0.53 Å = 0.53 × 10&sup-1;&sup0; m = 5.3 × 10&sup-1;¹ m
  • 1 light year = 9 460 800 000 000 000 m = 9.4608 × 10¹&sup5; m
  • 2.7 × 10&sup-4; torr = 0.00027 torr (already in scientific notation)

Significant figures are all the accurately known digits in a measurement plus the first doubtful digit.

Counting Significant Figures

  • 980 has 2 significant figures (a trailing zero without a decimal point is not counted)
  • 91.60 has 4 significant figures
  • 10010.100 has 8 significant figures
  • 0.0086 has 2 significant figures (leading zeros are not significant)

mcqs.q: All the accurately known digits plus the first doubtful digit in a measurement are called:
mcqs.why: Significant figures are all the digits known accurately plus the first doubtful digit. They show how precise a measurement is.

mcqs.q: 1 light year = 9 460 800 000 000 000 m. In scientific notation this is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Count the places the decimal point moves: 15 places to the left. Step 2: Write 9.4608 × 10¹&sup5; m. In scientific notation the digit part must lie between 1 and 10.

mcqs.q: The radius of the first orbit of the hydrogen atom, 0.53 Å, equals in metres:
mcqs.why: Step 1: 1 Å = 10&sup-1;&sup0; m, so 0.53 Å = 0.53 × 10&sup-1;&sup0; m. Step 2: Move the decimal one place: 0.53 × 10&sup-1;&sup0; = 5.3 × 10&sup-1;¹ m.

mcqs.q: How many significant figures are there in 980?
mcqs.why: In 980 the trailing zero has no decimal point before it, so it is not counted as significant. Only 9 and 8 count, giving 2 significant figures.

mcqs.q: How many significant figures are there in 91.60?
mcqs.why: All four digits count: 9, 1, 6 and the final 0, because a zero after a decimal point is significant. So 91.60 has 4 significant figures.

mcqs.q: How many significant figures are there in 10010.100?
mcqs.why: Every digit counts here, including the zeros between digits and the trailing zeros after the decimal point: 1,0,0,1,0,1,0,0 = 8 significant figures.

mcqs.q: How many significant figures are there in 0.0086?
mcqs.why: Leading zeros are never significant; they only fix the position of the decimal point. Only 8 and 6 count, so 0.0086 has 2 significant figures.

mcqs.q: 2.7 × 10&sup-4; torr written as an ordinary number is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: 10&sup-4; means move the decimal point 4 places to the left. Step 2: 2.7 × 10&sup-4; = 0.00027 torr.

mcqs.q: Significant figures in a measurement show:
options: the size of the measured quantity only
mcqs.why: The number of significant figures tells how precise the measurement is: more significant figures mean a more precise measurement, recorded with a better instrument.

mcqs.q: In scientific notation, a number is written as a digit part multiplied by a power of 10, where the digit part lies between:
mcqs.why: In standard scientific form the digit part (coefficient) must be at least 1 and less than 10, multiplied by a suitable power of 10, e.g. 5.3 × 10&sup-1;¹.

lessons.title: Measuring Instruments: Vernier Caliper, Screw Gauge and Stopwatch
lessons.notes_html:
The least count is the smallest measurement an instrument can make. A metre rule has a least count of 1 mm, a Vernier caliper 0.1 mm (0.01 cm) and a screw gauge (micrometer) 0.01 mm — so the screw gauge gives the most precise reading.

Vernier Caliper Reading

Reading = main-scale reading + (coinciding Vernier division × 0.01 cm)

Worked example: main scale = 6.5 cm, 5th Vernier division coincides.

Step 1: Vernier correction = 5 × 0.01 cm = 0.05 cm

Step 2: Total reading = 6.5 cm + 0.05 cm = 6.55 cm

Screw Gauge (Micrometer) Reading

Worked example: main scale = 6.5 mm, thimble division 13 coincides.

Step 1: Thimble value = 13 × 0.01 mm = 0.13 mm

Step 2: Total reading = 6.5 mm + 0.13 mm = 6.63 mm

Zero Error

If the zero of the Vernier scale falls exactly on the zero of the main scale, the zero error is zero. Zero error is a systematic error of the instrument.

Measuring Time

To time one oscillation of a pendulum accurately, time 10 oscillations and divide by 10 — this shrinks the effect of reaction-time error. A digital stopwatch (reading to 0.01 s) times the period still more accurately.

mcqs.q: In a Vernier scale diagram the main scale shows 6.5 cm and the 5th Vernier division coincides with a main-scale mark. The reading is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Main-scale reading = 6.5 cm. Step 2: Vernier correction = 5 × 0.01 cm = 0.05 cm. Step 3: Total = 6.5 + 0.05 = 6.55 cm.

mcqs.q: A micrometer (screw gauge) shows a main-scale reading of 6.5 mm and the 13th thimble division coincides. The reading is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Main-scale reading = 6.5 mm. Step 2: Thimble value = 13 × 0.01 mm = 0.13 mm. Step 3: Total = 6.5 + 0.13 = 6.63 mm.

mcqs.q: An engineer measures the width of an aluminium sheet with a Vernier caliper: main-scale reading 3.2 cm, 8th Vernier division coincides. The width is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Vernier correction = 8 × 0.01 cm = 0.08 cm. Step 2: Width = 3.2 cm + 0.08 cm = 3.28 cm.

mcqs.q: Which instrument gives the most precise reading?
mcqs.why: Precision depends on the least count. The screw gauge has the smallest least count (0.01 mm), smaller than the Vernier caliper (0.1 mm) and the metre rule (1 mm), so it is the most precise.

mcqs.q: When the zero mark of the Vernier scale falls exactly on the zero of the main scale, the zero error is:
mcqs.why: If the two zeros coincide exactly, there is no error to correct, so the zero error is zero. A shift to either side gives a positive or negative zero error.

mcqs.q: The zero error of an instrument is a:
mcqs.why: Zero error is built into the instrument and shifts every reading by the same amount, so it is a systematic error, not a random or human error.

mcqs.q: A pendulum swings from X to Y and back to X. The most accurate way to time one oscillation with a stopwatch is to:
options: time X to Y and double it
mcqs.why: Timing 10 oscillations and dividing by 10 spreads the reaction-time error over 10 swings, so the error in one period becomes 10 times smaller.

mcqs.q: An instrument that times the period of a pendulum more accurately than an ordinary stopwatch is:
mcqs.why: A digital stopwatch reads to 0.01 s (an electronic or photogate timer is even better), so it times the period more accurately than a hand-operated stopwatch.

mcqs.q: The least count of a Vernier caliper used in these readings is:
mcqs.why: Each Vernier division contributes 0.01 cm = 0.1 mm, which is the least count of the Vernier caliper. The screw gauge is finer still at 0.01 mm.

mcqs.q: The main scale of a Vernier caliper is:
mcqs.why: In a Vernier caliper the main scale is fixed in place, while the Vernier scale is the sliding scale that opens and closes the jaws for the reading.

lessons.title: Measuring Volume and Density
lessons.notes_html:
Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance:

Density = mass / volume

Its SI unit is kg m&sup-3;. The volume of an irregular solid is found with a measuring cylinder: the rise in the water level gives the volume of the object.

Worked Example 1

Ten identical steel balls, each of mass 27 g, are dropped into a cylinder holding 20 cm³ of water; the level rises to 50 cm³.

Step 1: Total mass = 10 × 27 g = 270 g

Step 2: Volume of the balls = 50 cm³ − 20 cm³ = 30 cm³

Step 3: Density = 270 g / 30 cm³ = 9.0 g/cm³

Worked Example 2

A 100 g object is dipped in water and the level moves from 50 cm³ to 90 cm³.

Step 1: Volume of the object = 90 cm³ − 50 cm³ = 40 cm³

Step 2: Density = 100 g / 40 cm³ = 2.5 g/cm³

Volumes of Regular Shapes (length = radius = 2 m)

  • Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³ = (4/3) × 3.14 × 8 = 33.5 m³
  • Cube: V = l³ = 8 m³
  • Cylinder: V = πr²l = 3.14 × 4 × 2 = 25.1 m³
  • Pyramid: V = (1/3)l²l = (1/3) × 4 × 2 = 2.67 m³

Density is a property of the material: it does not change with the shape of the piece.

mcqs.q: Ten identical steel balls, each of mass 27 g, raise the water level in a cylinder from 20 cm³ to 50 cm³. The density of the steel is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Total mass = 10 × 27 g = 270 g. Step 2: Volume = 50 − 20 = 30 cm³. Step 3: Density = 270 / 30 = 9.0 g/cm³.

mcqs.q: A 100 g object dipped in water moves the level from 50 cm³ to 90 cm³. The density of its material is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Volume of the object = 90 − 50 = 40 cm³. Step 2: Density = mass / volume = 100 / 40 = 2.5 g/cm³.

mcqs.q: A measuring cylinder holds 500 cc of water. A 20 g stone is dipped in and the level rises to 800 cc. The difference of the readings gives:
options: the final density of the water
mcqs.why: Step 1: Difference = 800 cc − 500 cc = 300 cc. Step 2: This rise in level is the volume of the stone. Density would need mass / volume = 20 / 300 = 0.067 g/cc as a further step.

mcqs.q: Density is defined as:
mcqs.why: Density = mass / volume. It tells how much mass is packed into each unit volume of a substance, with SI unit kg m&sup-3;.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of density is:
mcqs.why: Density = mass (kg) / volume (m³), so its SI unit is kg m&sup-3;. The unit g/cm³ is also used, but it is not the SI unit.

mcqs.q: The volume of a sphere of radius 2 m is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: V = (4/3)πr³. Step 2: V = (4/3) × 3.14 × (2 m)³ = (4/3) × 3.14 × 8 = 33.5 m³.

mcqs.q: The volume of a cube of side 2 m is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: V = l³. Step 2: V = (2 m)³ = 8 m³. The side length is cubed, not multiplied by 3.

mcqs.q: The volume of a cylinder of radius 2 m and length 2 m is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: V = πr²l. Step 2: V = 3.14 × (2 m)² × 2 m = 3.14 × 4 × 2 = 25.1 m³.

mcqs.q: A block of wood of mass 1 kg is shaped as a sphere (volume 33.5 m³) or as a cube (volume 8 m³). Does the density of wood change with shape?
options: Yes, the cube is less dense
No, density is a property of the material
mcqs.why: Density belongs to the material, not the shape. The two quick calculations differ only because the same 1 kg mass was forced into two different volumes; a real piece would have different masses and the same density.

mcqs.q: The volume of an irregular solid is measured with a measuring cylinder by:
options: measuring its length with a rule
the rise in the liquid level when the solid is dipped in
mcqs.why: The solid pushes aside (displaces) its own volume of liquid, so the rise in the level of the measuring cylinder equals the volume of the solid.

lessons.title: Rest, Motion and Relative Motion
lessons.notes_html:
Rest and Motion

  • Rest: a body is said to be at rest if it does not change its position with respect to its surroundings.
  • Motion: a body is said to be in motion if it changes its position with respect to its surroundings.

Relative Motion

Relative motion is the motion of a body measured with respect to another moving body (or reference point). For example, a passenger sitting in a moving bus is at rest relative to the bus but in motion relative to the road.

What Is Kinematics?

Kinematics is derived from the Greek word 'kinema'. It is the study of how an object changes its position in space in a certain time interval, without considering the causes of motion.

mcqs.q: A body is said to be at rest if:
options: it does not change its position with respect to its surroundings
mcqs.why: Rest means the position of the body does not change with respect to its surroundings. A body can be at rest relative to one surrounding and moving relative to another.

mcqs.q: A body is said to be in motion if:
options: it changes its position with respect to its surroundings
mcqs.why: Motion is the change of position of a body with respect to its surroundings with time. If the position does not change, the body is at rest.

mcqs.q: Relative motion is the motion of a body measured:
options: with respect to another moving body or reference point
mcqs.why: Motion is always described relative to some reference. Relative motion is measured with respect to another moving body or a chosen reference point.

mcqs.q: A passenger sitting in a moving bus is:
options: in motion relative to the bus
at rest relative to the road
at rest relative to the bus but in motion relative to the road
mcqs.why: The passenger does not change position inside the bus, so he is at rest relative to the bus. But he moves along with the bus, so he is in motion relative to the road.

mcqs.q: Kinematics is the study of motion:
options: without considering the causes of motion
mcqs.why: Kinematics describes how position changes with time — distance, displacement, speed and acceleration — without considering the forces that cause the motion. Causes are studied in dynamics.

mcqs.q: The word 'kinematics' is derived from the Greek word:
mcqs.why: Kinematics comes from the Greek word 'kinema', which relates to motion. The word physics comes from 'physicos', meaning knowledge of nature.

mcqs.q: Two objects can be at rest relative to each other while both are in motion relative to the ground. This is because motion is:
mcqs.why: Motion and rest are relative terms: they depend on the reference chosen. Passengers in the same bus are at rest relative to each other but in motion relative to the road.

mcqs.q: Which of the following quantities does kinematics deal with?
mcqs.why: Kinematics is about describing motion itself: distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration. Force and its effects belong to dynamics.

mcqs.q: A book lying on a table in a moving train is at rest with respect to:
mcqs.why: The book does not change its position inside the train, so it is at rest relative to the train, even though it is moving relative to the ground.

mcqs.q: Whether a body is at rest or in motion depends on:
mcqs.why: Rest and motion are judged with respect to the surroundings. Change the reference and the same body may be described as at rest or in motion.

lessons.title: Scalar and Vector Quantities
lessons.notes_html:
Scalar quantities are completely specified by magnitude and a suitable unit, e.g. mass, time, distance, speed.

Vector quantities need magnitude, a suitable unit and a particular direction, e.g. displacement, velocity, force, weight.

How a Vector Is Represented

A vector is drawn as an arrow: the length of the arrow (to a chosen scale) shows its magnitude, and the arrowhead shows its direction.

mcqs.q: Scalar quantities have ______ and a suitable unit.
mcqs.why: A scalar is completely described by its magnitude (size) and a suitable unit, e.g. mass = 5 kg. No direction is needed for a scalar.

mcqs.q: Vector quantities have ______ along with magnitude and unit.
mcqs.why: A vector needs three things: magnitude, a suitable unit and a particular direction, e.g. a force of 10 N towards the east.

mcqs.q: Which one is a vector quantity?
mcqs.why: Weight is the pull of gravity on a body and acts in a direction (towards the Earth), so it is a vector. Mass, time and distance are scalars.

mcqs.q: Which one is a scalar quantity?
mcqs.why: Time has magnitude and unit only, so it is a scalar. Force, velocity and displacement all need a direction and are vectors.

mcqs.q: Distance is a ______ quantity.
mcqs.why: Distance is the total length of the path covered; it has magnitude and unit but no direction, so it is a scalar quantity.

mcqs.q: A vector quantity is represented graphically by:
options: a straight line without a head
an arrow whose length shows magnitude and whose head shows direction
mcqs.why: Vectors are drawn as arrows: the length of the arrow (to a chosen scale) represents the magnitude, and the arrowhead points in the direction of the quantity.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a vector?
mcqs.why: Velocity is displacement per unit time in a stated direction, so it is a vector. Speed, mass and temperature are scalars.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a scalar?
mcqs.why: Speed is distance covered per unit time; it has magnitude and unit but no direction, so it is a scalar. Displacement, weight and force are vectors.

mcqs.q: To describe a vector completely, we must state:
mcqs.why: A vector is only completely specified when its magnitude, a suitable unit and its particular direction are all given, e.g. velocity 20 m/s towards north.

mcqs.q: The length of the arrow drawn for a vector shows its:
mcqs.why: In the arrow representation of a vector, the length (drawn to a chosen scale) shows the magnitude, while the arrowhead shows the direction.

lessons.title: Distance, Displacement, Speed and Velocity
lessons.notes_html:
Distance and Displacement

  • Distance is the total length of the path covered by a moving body. It is a scalar and is never negative.
  • Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from the starting point to the end point in a stated direction. It is a vector and can be zero even when distance is not zero.

Speed and Velocity

Speed = distance / time

Velocity = displacement / time

  • Speed is a scalar; its unit is m/s.
  • Velocity is a vector; its unit is m/s in a stated direction.

mcqs.q: The shortest distance between two points is called:
mcqs.why: Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from the start point to the end point, together with its direction. Distance is the full length of the path actually travelled.

mcqs.q: What is the SI unit of velocity?
mcqs.why: Velocity = displacement / time, so its SI unit is metre per second, written ms&sup-1; (m/s). The unit ms&sup-2; belongs to acceleration.

mcqs.q: Speed is defined as:
mcqs.why: Speed is the rate of change of distance: speed = distance / time. Velocity, by contrast, is the rate of change of displacement.

mcqs.q: Velocity is defined as:
mcqs.why: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement: velocity = displacement / time, measured in m/s in a stated direction.

mcqs.q: Distance differs from displacement because distance:
options: is the total path length and is never negative
is always zero on a round trip
mcqs.why: Distance is the total length of the path covered and is never negative. Displacement is the shortest straight-line change of position and can be zero or negative.

mcqs.q: A body completes a full round trip and returns to its starting point. Its displacement is:
mcqs.why: Displacement depends only on the start and end points. In a round trip both points are the same, so displacement = 0, even though the distance covered is not zero.

mcqs.q: Speed is a scalar quantity because it has:
options: magnitude and unit but no direction
mcqs.why: Speed tells how fast a body moves (magnitude) in a unit (m/s), but it does not tell the direction of motion, so it is a scalar.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of speed is the same as that of:
mcqs.why: Both speed and velocity are measured in metres per second (m/s). Acceleration is m/s², force is the newton and momentum is kg m/s.

mcqs.q: If a car covers 100 m in 5 s, its average speed is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Speed = distance / time. Step 2: Speed = 100 m / 5 s = 20 m/s.

mcqs.q: Displacement is a vector quantity because it needs:
options: a stated direction along with magnitude and unit
mcqs.why: Displacement is the shortest distance from start to end point in a stated direction, so it needs magnitude, unit and direction — the marks of a vector.

lessons.title: Acceleration
lessons.notes_html:
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with respect to time:

a = (vf − vi) / t

Its SI unit is m/s² (ms&sup-2;) and it is a vector quantity.

Worked Example

A bus speeds up from 20 ms&sup-1; to 40 ms&sup-1; in 8 s. Find its acceleration.

Step 1: Change of velocity = vf − vi = 40 ms&sup-1; − 20 ms&sup-1; = 20 ms&sup-1;

Step 2: a = change of velocity / time = 20 ms&sup-1; / 8 s

Step 3: a = 2.5 ms&sup-2;

mcqs.q: What is the SI unit of acceleration?
mcqs.why: Acceleration = change of velocity / time = (m/s) / s = m/s², written ms&sup-2;. The unit ms&sup-1; is for velocity.

mcqs.q: Acceleration is defined as:
mcqs.why: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with respect to time: a = (v<sub>f</sub> − v<sub>i</sub>) / t. Its SI unit is m/s².

mcqs.q: A bus speeds up from 20 ms&sup-1; to 40 ms&sup-1; in 8 s. Its acceleration is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: a = (v<sub>f</sub> − v<sub>i</sub>) / t. Step 2: a = (40 − 20) / 8 = 20 / 8. Step 3: a = 2.5 ms&sup-2;.

mcqs.q: Acceleration is a vector quantity because:
mcqs.why: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, and velocity is a vector. So acceleration also has magnitude, unit and direction — it is a vector.

mcqs.q: If a body's velocity does not change, its acceleration is:
mcqs.why: Acceleration = change of velocity / time. If the velocity stays the same, the change is zero, so the acceleration is zero.

mcqs.q: A car slows down from 30 ms&sup-1; to 10 ms&sup-1; in 5 s. Its acceleration is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: a = (v<sub>f</sub> − v<sub>i</sub>) / t = (10 − 30) / 5. Step 2: a = −20 / 5 = −4 ms&sup-2;. The negative sign shows the car is slowing down (retardation).

mcqs.q: In the formula a = (v<sub>f</sub> − v<sub>i</sub>) / t, the symbol v<sub>i</sub> stands for:
mcqs.why: v<sub>i</sub> is the initial velocity (velocity at the start) and v<sub>f</sub> is the final velocity. The difference v<sub>f</sub> − v<sub>i</sub> is the change of velocity.

mcqs.q: A body starts from rest and reaches 25 ms&sup-1; in 5 s. Its acceleration is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Starting from rest, v<sub>i</sub> = 0. Step 2: a = (25 − 0) / 5 = 25 / 5. Step 3: a = 5 ms&sup-2;.

mcqs.q: Negative acceleration is also called:
mcqs.why: When a body slows down, its final velocity is less than its initial velocity, so the acceleration comes out negative. This negative acceleration is called retardation or deceleration.

mcqs.q: Which of the following has the unit ms&sup-2;?
mcqs.why: Acceleration is measured in metres per second squared (ms&sup-2;), because it is the change of velocity (ms&sup-1;) per second. Velocity and speed use ms&sup-1;.

lessons.title: Equations of Motion
lessons.notes_html:
For uniformly accelerated motion the book uses these relations:

vf = vi + at

S = vit + ½at²

vf² = vi² + 2aS

Worked Example 1

A bus travels at 15 ms&sup-1; and speeds up at 5 ms&sup-2;. Find its final velocity after 6 s.

Step 1: vf = vi + at

Step 2: vf = 15 ms&sup-1; + (5 ms&sup-2; × 6 s) = 15 + 30

Step 3: vf = 45 ms&sup-1;

Worked Example 2

A car starts from rest with acceleration 5 ms&sup-2;. Find the time to travel 50 m.

Step 1: S = vit + ½at² with vi = 0 gives 50 m = ½ × 5 ms&sup-2; × t²

Step 2: 50 = 2.5 t², so t² = 20

Step 3: t = 4.47 s (about 4.5 s)

mcqs.q: A bus travels at 15 ms&sup-1; and speeds up at 5 ms&sup-2;. Its final velocity after 6 s is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: v<sub>f</sub> = v<sub>i</sub> + at. Step 2: v<sub>f</sub> = 15 + 5 × 6 = 15 + 30. Step 3: v<sub>f</sub> = 45 ms&sup-1;.

mcqs.q: A car starts from rest with an acceleration of 5 ms&sup-2;. The time it takes to travel 50 m is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: S = v<sub>i</sub>t + ½at² = 0 + ½ × 5 × t². Step 2: 50 = 2.5 t², so t² = 20. Step 3: t = √20 = 4.47 s.

mcqs.q: The first equation of motion is:
mcqs.why: The first equation of motion, v<sub>f</sub> = v<sub>i</sub> + at, links final velocity, initial velocity, acceleration and time. It comes directly from the definition of acceleration.

mcqs.q: The equation S = v<sub>i</sub>t + ½at² is used to find:
options: final velocity when time is unknown
distance covered in a given time
mcqs.why: This second equation of motion gives the distance S covered in time t by a body starting with velocity v<sub>i</sub> and acceleration a.

mcqs.q: A body starts from rest (v<sub>i</sub> = 0) with acceleration 2 ms&sup-2;. Its velocity after 10 s is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: v<sub>f</sub> = v<sub>i</sub> + at = 0 + 2 × 10. Step 2: v<sub>f</sub> = 20 ms&sup-1;. Starting from rest, the initial velocity is zero.

mcqs.q: In the equations of motion, the symbol S stands for:
mcqs.why: S stands for the distance (displacement) covered by the body during the motion. Speed is written v, and time is written t.

mcqs.q: The third equation of motion, v<sub>f</sub>² = v<sub>i</sub>² + 2aS, is most useful when:
options: time is not given and not required
mcqs.why: The third equation links velocities, acceleration and distance without using time, so it is used when time is neither given nor asked for.

mcqs.q: A bike moving at 10 ms&sup-1; accelerates at 2 ms&sup-2; for 4 s. The distance covered is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: S = v<sub>i</sub>t + ½at² = 10 × 4 + ½ × 2 × 4². Step 2: S = 40 + 16 = 56 m.

mcqs.q: Equations of motion apply to bodies moving with:
mcqs.why: The equations v<sub>f</sub> = v<sub>i</sub> + at, S = v<sub>i</sub>t + ½at² and v<sub>f</sub>² = v<sub>i</sub>² + 2aS are derived for uniform (constant) acceleration.

mcqs.q: A stone dropped from rest falls with a = 10 ms&sup-2;. Using v<sub>f</sub> = v<sub>i</sub> + at, its velocity after 3 s is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: v<sub>i</sub> = 0 (dropped from rest), a = 10 ms&sup-2;, t = 3 s. Step 2: v<sub>f</sub> = 0 + 10 × 3 = 30 ms&sup-1;.

lessons.title: Motion under Gravity (Free Fall)
lessons.notes_html:
Motion under gravity is the motion of a body under the pull of the Earth alone (free fall), in which it accelerates downward with:

g = 10 ms&sup-2;

By convention the upward direction is taken as positive. Gravity always acts downward, opposite to upward motion, so for an upward-moving object g is taken as negative (g = −10 ms&sup-2;).

Worked Example 1: Dropped Ball

A ball is dropped from a height of 50 m. Find its velocity just before touching the ground.

Step 1: vf² = vi² + 2gS = 0 + 2 × 10 ms&sup-2; × 50 m

Step 2: vf² = 1000

Step 3: vf = 31.6 ms&sup-1; downward

Worked Example 2: Thrown Upward

A body is thrown upward with velocity 50 ms&sup-1;. Find the maximum height.

Step 1: At the highest point vf = 0, and g = −10 ms&sup-2;

Step 2: 0 = (50 ms&sup-1;)² − 2 × 10 ms&sup-2; × S, so 20S = 2500

Step 3: S = 125 m

Worked Example 3: Time of Fall

A ball falls from the top of a height of 70 m. Find the time to reach the ground.

Step 1: S = vit + ½gt² gives 70 m = ½ × 10 ms&sup-2; × t²

Step 2: 70 = 5t², so t² = 14

Step 3: t = 3.74 s (about 3.7 s)

mcqs.q: Motion under gravity is the motion of a body:
options: under the pull of the Earth alone, accelerating downward with g = 10 ms&sup-2;
mcqs.why: In free fall the only force is the Earth's pull, so the body accelerates downward at g = 10 ms&sup-2;. This is called motion under gravity.

mcqs.q: For an object moving upward, gravity is taken as negative because:
options: the object has no mass upward
the upward direction is taken as positive and gravity acts downward, opposite to the motion
mcqs.why: By convention upward is positive. Gravity always pulls downward, opposite to the upward motion, so g = −10 ms&sup-2; for a body moving upward.

mcqs.q: A ball is dropped from a height of 50 m. Its velocity just before touching the ground is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: v<sub>f</sub>² = v<sub>i</sub>² + 2gS = 0 + 2 × 10 × 50 = 1000. Step 2: v<sub>f</sub> = √1000 = 31.6 ms&sup-1; downward.

mcqs.q: A body is thrown upward with a velocity of 50 ms&sup-1;. The maximum height it reaches is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: At the top v<sub>f</sub> = 0 and g = −10 ms&sup-2;. Step 2: 0 = 50² − 20S, so S = 2500 / 20. Step 3: S = 125 m.

mcqs.q: A ball falls from the top of a height of 70 m. The time it takes to reach the ground is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: S = ½gt² gives 70 = ½ × 10 × t² = 5t². Step 2: t² = 14. Step 3: t = √14 = 3.74 s.

mcqs.q: The value of g used for freely falling bodies in this book is:
mcqs.why: For free-fall problems the book takes the acceleration due to gravity as g = 10 ms&sup-2;. The value 1.6 ms&sup-2; is g on the Moon.

mcqs.q: At the highest point of a body thrown vertically upward, its velocity is:
mcqs.why: The body slows down as it rises against gravity and stops for an instant at the highest point, so v<sub>f</sub> = 0 there, before it starts falling back.

mcqs.q: A ball dropped from a height of 20 m reaches the ground with velocity:
mcqs.why: Step 1: v<sub>f</sub>² = 0 + 2gS = 2 × 10 × 20 = 400. Step 2: v<sub>f</sub> = √400 = 20 ms&sup-1; downward.

mcqs.q: For a freely falling body, the equations of motion are used with the acceleration a replaced by:
mcqs.why: In free fall the acceleration is the acceleration due to gravity, so a = g = 10 ms&sup-2; (negative when the body is moving upward).

mcqs.q: A body thrown upward with velocity 30 ms&sup-1; reaches a maximum height of:
mcqs.why: Step 1: 0 = v<sub>i</sub>² − 2gS = 30² − 20S. Step 2: S = 900 / 20 = 45 m.

lessons.title: Newton's First Law of Motion and Inertia
lessons.notes_html:
Newton's first law: a body remains in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless an unbalanced external force acts on it. It is also known as the law of inertia.

Examples

  • A book lying on a table stays at rest.
  • A ball rolling on smooth ground keeps rolling until friction stops it.
  • Passengers lurch forward when a moving bus suddenly stops.

Common Observations Caused by Inertia

  • Dust comes off a carpet when it is beaten.
  • A coin drops into a glass when the card under it is flicked away.
  • A passenger falls backward when a bus suddenly starts.
  • A hammer head tightens on its handle when the handle is struck on the ground.

Dynamics is the study of the cause of motion: force, mass and the frictional force that affects the motion of an object.

mcqs.q: Newton's first law of motion is also known as the law of:
mcqs.why: Newton's first law says a body keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless an unbalanced force acts. This tendency to resist change is inertia, so it is called the law of inertia.

mcqs.q: According to Newton's first law, a body remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted on by:
mcqs.why: The first law states that only an unbalanced external force can change a body's state of rest or uniform straight-line motion.

mcqs.q: Passengers lurch forward when a moving bus suddenly stops. This is due to:
mcqs.why: The passengers' bodies keep moving forward with the bus's earlier motion (inertia of motion) even though the bus has stopped, so they lurch forward.

mcqs.q: Dust comes off a carpet when it is beaten because:
options: the dust is glued to the carpet
the carpet moves but the dust stays in place due to inertia of rest
mcqs.why: When the carpet is beaten it moves suddenly, but the dust particles tend to stay at rest (inertia of rest), so they separate from the carpet and fall off.

mcqs.q: A coin drops into a glass when the card under it is flicked away because:
options: the coin stays at rest due to inertia while the card moves away
the coin is pulled by the card
the coin flies with the card
mcqs.why: The flicked card moves away quickly, but the coin tends to remain at rest due to inertia, so it loses support and falls into the glass under gravity.

mcqs.q: A passenger falls backward when a bus suddenly starts because:
options: his body tends to remain at rest while the bus moves forward
mcqs.why: At the start, the lower body moves with the bus but the upper body tends to stay at rest (inertia of rest), so the passenger falls backward.

mcqs.q: A ball rolling on smooth ground keeps rolling until it stops. It finally stops because of:
mcqs.why: By the first law the ball would roll forever, but friction (an unbalanced external force) acts against its motion and brings it to rest.

mcqs.q: Inertia is the property of a body by which it resists a change in its:
options: state of rest or uniform motion
mcqs.why: Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line. It depends on the mass of the body.

mcqs.q: A hammer head tightens on its handle when the handle's end is struck on the ground because:
options: the handle stops suddenly but the head keeps moving down due to inertia
mcqs.why: When the handle hits the ground it stops suddenly; the loose head continues moving downward due to inertia and wedges tightly onto the handle.

mcqs.q: Dynamics is the study of:
options: the cause of motion — force, mass and friction
mcqs.why: Dynamics studies the cause of motion. Force, the mass of the object and the frictional force all affect the motion of an object, and Newton's laws govern them.

lessons.title: Newton's Second Law: Force, Mass and Acceleration
lessons.notes_html:
Newton's second law: the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force. For a fixed mass this gives:

F = ma

For a fixed mass, the acceleration produced is directly proportional to the applied force (a ∝ F).

Worked Example 1

A force of 3400 N is applied to a body of mass 850 kg. Find the acceleration.

Step 1: a = F / m

Step 2: a = 3400 N / 850 kg

Step 3: a = 4 ms&sup-2;

To produce the same acceleration in a body of mass 425 kg: F = ma = 425 kg × 4 ms&sup-2; = 1700 N.

Worked Example 2

Find the mass of a body accelerated by a force of 200 N with acceleration 36 ms&sup-2;.

Step 1: m = F / a

Step 2: m = 200 N / 36 ms&sup-2; = 5.56 kg

If the force changes to 280 N: a = F / m = 280 N / 5.56 kg = 50.4 ms&sup-2;.

Worked Example 3

An empty car of mass 1200 kg is accelerated at 4 ms&sup-2; by its engine. A 300 kg load is added. Find the new acceleration.

Step 1: Engine force F = ma = 1200 kg × 4 ms&sup-2; = 4800 N

Step 2: New mass = 1200 kg + 300 kg = 1500 kg

Step 3: a = F / m = 4800 N / 1500 kg = 3.2 ms&sup-2;

mcqs.q: It is easier to push an empty shopping cart than a full one, because the filled cart has more mass. For the same acceleration this is expressed by:
mcqs.why: From F = ma, for the same acceleration the force needed is directly proportional to the mass (F ∝ m). The fuller cart has more mass, so it needs more force.

mcqs.q: Newton's second law gives the relation:
mcqs.why: Newton's second law — rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force — reduces for a fixed mass to F = ma: force = mass × acceleration.

mcqs.q: A force of 3400 N is applied to a body of mass 850 kg. The acceleration produced is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: a = F / m. Step 2: a = 3400 N / 850 kg. Step 3: a = 4 ms&sup-2;.

mcqs.q: How much force should be applied to a body of mass 425 kg to produce an acceleration of 4 ms&sup-2;?
mcqs.why: Step 1: F = ma. Step 2: F = 425 kg × 4 ms&sup-2;. Step 3: F = 1700 N.

mcqs.q: A body is accelerated by a force of 200 N at 36 ms&sup-2;. Its mass is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: m = F / a. Step 2: m = 200 N / 36 ms&sup-2;. Step 3: m = 5.56 kg.

mcqs.q: The same body (mass 5.56 kg) is acted on by a force of 280 N. Its new acceleration is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: a = F / m. Step 2: a = 280 N / 5.56 kg. Step 3: a = 50.4 ms&sup-2;. For a fixed mass, acceleration is proportional to force.

mcqs.q: An engine accelerates an empty 1200 kg car at 4 ms&sup-2;. With a 300 kg load added, the same engine produces:
mcqs.why: Step 1: F = 1200 × 4 = 4800 N. Step 2: New mass = 1500 kg. Step 3: a = 4800 / 1500 = 3.2 ms&sup-2;. More mass with the same force means less acceleration.

mcqs.q: A man pulls a crate of mass 25 kg with a horizontal force of 60 N against a constant friction force of 20 N. The acceleration of the crate is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Net force = 60 N − 20 N = 40 N. Step 2: a = F / m = 40 N / 25 kg. Step 3: a = 1.6 ms&sup-2;. Only the net (unbalanced) force produces acceleration.

mcqs.q: For a fixed mass, the acceleration produced is:
options: directly proportional to the applied force
mcqs.why: From F = ma with m fixed, a = F / m, so acceleration is directly proportional to the applied force: double the force and the acceleration doubles.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of force, the newton, is equal to:
mcqs.why: From F = ma, 1 N = 1 kg × 1 ms&sup-2; = 1 kg ms&sup-2;: the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 ms&sup-2;.

lessons.title: Momentum and Conservation of Momentum
lessons.notes_html:
Momentum is the product of mass and velocity:

p = mv

Its SI unit is kg ms&sup-1; (also written Ns). Momentum is a vector quantity.

Law of conservation of momentum: the total momentum of a system of bodies before a collision remains the same (constant) after the collision, provided no external force acts.

Worked Example 1

Find the momentum of a body of mass 6 kg moving with velocity 25 ms&sup-1;.

Step 1: p = mv = 6 kg × 25 ms&sup-1;

Step 2: p = 150 kg ms&sup-1;

If the momentum becomes 200 Ns: v = p / m = 200 / 6 = 33.3 ms&sup-1;.

Worked Example 2

A body of mass 10 kg moves at 10 ms&sup-1;. A force acts for 5 s and reduces its velocity to 2 ms&sup-1;.

Step 1: Momentum before = 10 kg × 10 ms&sup-1; = 100 kg ms&sup-1;

Step 2: Momentum after = 10 kg × 2 ms&sup-1; = 20 kg ms&sup-1;

Safety and Momentum

The wire grill (fence) in front of a batsman's helmet shields the face while letting him see the ball. It spreads the impact of the ball over the grill and helmet and stops the ball from striking the face, eyes and nose directly, so injuries are prevented. Safety devices such as packaging of fragile objects, crumple zones and seatbelts reduce the effects of changing momentum.

Newton's Third Law and the Earth

When a falling object is pulled by the Earth, the object also pulls the Earth with an equal and opposite force (third law). The Earth does move towards the object, but its acceleration (a = F / M) is vanishingly small because the Earth's mass is enormous, so the movement cannot be observed.

mcqs.q: The quantity of motion contained in a body is called:
mcqs.why: The quantity of motion in a body is its momentum, p = mv. A heavier or faster body has more momentum than a lighter or slower one.

mcqs.q: The law of conservation of momentum states that the total momentum of a system of two bodies before and after collision:
mcqs.why: By the law of conservation of momentum, the total momentum before a collision equals the total momentum after it, as long as no external force acts on the system.

mcqs.q: Momentum is calculated by the equation:
mcqs.why: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity: p = mv. Its SI unit is kg ms&sup-1;, also written as Ns.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of momentum is:
mcqs.why: Momentum = kg × m/s, so its SI unit is kg ms&sup-1;, which is the same as the newton-second (Ns).

mcqs.q: Find the momentum of a body of mass 6 kg moving with a velocity of 25 ms&sup-1;.
mcqs.why: Step 1: p = mv. Step 2: p = 6 kg × 25 ms&sup-1;. Step 3: p = 150 kg ms&sup-1;.

mcqs.q: If the momentum of the same 6 kg body becomes 200 Ns, its velocity will be:
mcqs.why: Step 1: v = p / m. Step 2: v = 200 Ns / 6 kg. Step 3: v = 33.3 ms&sup-1;.

mcqs.q: A body of mass 10 kg moves at 10 ms&sup-1;. A force reduces its velocity to 2 ms&sup-1;. Its momentum before and after is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Before: p = 10 × 10 = 100 kg ms&sup-1;. Step 2: After: p = 10 × 2 = 20 kg ms&sup-1;. The force changed the body's momentum.

mcqs.q: When a falling object is pulled towards the Earth, does the Earth also move towards the object?
options: Yes, with the same acceleration as the object
Yes, but its acceleration is vanishingly small because its mass is enormous
mcqs.why: By Newton's third law the object pulls the Earth with an equal and opposite force. But a = F / M is tiny for the Earth's huge mass M, so the Earth's movement cannot be observed.

mcqs.q: The wire grill of a batsman's helmet prevents injuries because it:
options: spreads the impact over the grill and helmet and stops the ball striking the face directly
makes the ball bounce back faster
hides the ball from the batsman
mcqs.why: The grill shields the face, eyes and nose: it spreads the ball's impact over a larger area and stops the ball from hitting the face directly, while still letting the batsman see the ball.

mcqs.q: Force can also be written in terms of momentum as: Force = change in momentum / ______.
mcqs.why: Newton's second law says force equals the rate of change of momentum: F = change in momentum / time taken. This is why spreading an impact over more time reduces the force.

lessons.title: Mass and Weight
lessons.notes_html:
Differences Between Mass and Weight

MassWeight
Quantity of matter in a bodyPull of gravity on the body
Scalar quantityVector quantity
Measured in kilograms (kg)Measured in newtons (N)
Same everywhereChanges from place to place with g

Weight is calculated by:

W = mg

Worked Example

The mass of an object is 60 kg. Find its weight on Earth, the Moon and Mars (g: Earth 9.8 ms&sup-2;, Moon 1.6 ms&sup-2;, Mars 3.7 ms&sup-2;).

Step 1 (Earth): W = 60 kg × 9.8 ms&sup-2; = 588 N

Step 2 (Moon): W = 60 kg × 1.6 ms&sup-2; = 96 N

Step 3 (Mars): W = 60 kg × 3.7 ms&sup-2; = 222 N

mcqs.q: The quantity of matter contained in a body is called ______.
mcqs.why: Mass is the quantity of matter contained in a body. It is measured in kilograms and remains the same everywhere.

mcqs.q: The weight of a body can be measured using a spring balance; it differs from place to place because of variation in ______.
mcqs.why: Weight W = mg depends on g. The gravitational pull (g) is not the same everywhere, so the weight measured by a spring balance changes from place to place.

mcqs.q: Weight is calculated by the equation:
mcqs.why: Weight is the gravitational force on a mass: W = mg, where m is the mass in kg and g is the acceleration due to gravity in ms&sup-2;.

mcqs.q: An object of mass 60 kg has weight on Earth (g = 9.8 ms&sup-2;) equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: W = mg. Step 2: W = 60 kg × 9.8 ms&sup-2;. Step 3: W = 588 N.

mcqs.q: The weight of the same 60 kg object on the Moon (g = 1.6 ms&sup-2;) is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: W = mg. Step 2: W = 60 kg × 1.6 ms&sup-2;. Step 3: W = 96 N. The mass stays 60 kg; only the weight changes with g.

mcqs.q: The weight of a 60 kg object on Mars (g = 3.7 ms&sup-2;) is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: W = mg. Step 2: W = 60 kg × 3.7 ms&sup-2;. Step 3: W = 222 N.

mcqs.q: Which statement about mass is correct?
options: Mass is the quantity of matter and is the same everywhere
Mass changes from place to place
mcqs.why: Mass is a scalar measure of the quantity of matter in a body, measured in kilograms. It does not change with place; weight is the one that changes.

mcqs.q: Weight is a vector quantity because it:
options: acts in a direction (towards the Earth)
mcqs.why: Weight is a force — the pull of gravity — and forces act in a direction (towards the centre of the Earth), so weight is a vector measured in newtons.

mcqs.q: Mass is measured in ______ and weight is measured in ______.
mcqs.why: Mass is measured in kilograms (kg) with a beam balance, while weight, being a force, is measured in newtons (N) with a spring balance.

mcqs.q: If g at a place becomes smaller, the weight of a body there will:
mcqs.why: Since W = mg and the mass m is fixed, a smaller g gives a smaller weight. That is why weight on the Moon is about one-sixth of the weight on Earth.

lessons.title: Circular Motion, Centripetal and Centrifugal Force
lessons.notes_html:
An object moving in a circle is acted on by forces towards and away from the centre:

  • Centripetal force acts towards the centre of the circle and keeps the object moving in its circular path.
  • Centrifugal force is the apparent outward force felt in the rotating frame, acting away from the centre.

Fc = mv² / r

ac = v² / r

In a diagram: draw a circle with centre O; at a point on the circle draw the velocity arrow along the tangent, the centripetal force arrow pointing from the point towards O, and the centrifugal force arrow pointing away from O.

Worked Example

A car of mass 600 kg runs on a circular part of a highway of radius about 1000 m at 72 km/h. Find the centripetal force and the centripetal acceleration.

Step 1: v = 72 km/h = 72 × 1000 / 3600 = 20 ms&sup-1;

Step 2: Fc = mv² / r = 600 kg × (20 ms&sup-1;)² / 1000 m = 600 × 400 / 1000 = 240 N

Step 3: ac = v² / r = 400 / 1000 = 0.4 ms&sup-2;

Uses of the Centrifuge

  • Cream separator (separating cream from milk)
  • Washing-machine dryer
  • Laboratory centrifuge for blood and urine tests
  • Separation of isotopes and DNA samples

mcqs.q: Centrifugal force is always directed:
mcqs.why: Centrifugal force is the apparent outward force, directed away from the centre of the circle. Centripetal force is the inward one, towards the centre.

mcqs.q: Centripetal force acts:
options: towards the centre of the circle
mcqs.why: Centripetal force points towards the centre of the circle and keeps the object moving along its circular path instead of flying off along the tangent.

mcqs.q: The centripetal force on a body moving in a circle is given by:
mcqs.why: For circular motion the required centripetal force is F<sub>c</sub> = mv² / r, where m is the mass, v the speed and r the radius of the circle.

mcqs.q: A car of mass 600 kg moves at 72 km/h on a circular path of radius 1000 m. The centripetal force is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: v = 72 × 1000 / 3600 = 20 ms&sup-1;. Step 2: F<sub>c</sub> = mv² / r = 600 × 400 / 1000. Step 3: F<sub>c</sub> = 240 N.

mcqs.q: The centripetal acceleration of the same car is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: a<sub>c</sub> = v² / r. Step 2: a<sub>c</sub> = (20 ms&sup-1;)² / 1000 m = 400 / 1000. Step 3: a<sub>c</sub> = 0.4 ms&sup-2;.

mcqs.q: The velocity of a body moving in a circle is directed:
options: along the tangent to the circle
mcqs.why: At every point of a circular path the velocity is along the tangent to the circle. The centripetal force, by contrast, points from the body towards the centre.

mcqs.q: 72 km/h is equal to:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Multiply by 1000 to change km to m and divide by 3600 to change hours to seconds. Step 2: 72 × 1000 / 3600 = 20 ms&sup-1;.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a useful everyday use of the centrifuge?
mcqs.why: A cream separator is a centrifuge: spinning throws the heavier milk outward and collects the lighter cream near the centre. Centrifuges are also used in washing-machine dryers and laboratories.

mcqs.q: In the 'death well', the biker does not fall because:
options: the wall supplies the centripetal force and friction balances his weight
mcqs.why: In the death well the wall pushes the biker towards the centre (centripetal force), and friction between the tyres and the wall balances his weight, so he stays up while circling.

mcqs.q: If the speed of a body in circular motion doubles (same radius), the centripetal force becomes:
mcqs.why: F<sub>c</sub> = mv² / r depends on v². Doubling v makes v² four times bigger, so the centripetal force becomes four times as large.

lessons.title: Friction
lessons.notes_html:
Friction is the force that opposes motion between two surfaces in contact. It arises because of the roughness of the surfaces.

Kinds of Friction

The limiting frictional force (maximum static friction) is greater than rolling friction, sliding friction and kinetic friction. Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction.

Fs = μmg

Worked Example

A block of mass 15 kg is placed on a wet slippery floor. When pulled through a string and spring balance, it shows a force of 3 N. Find the coefficient of friction.

Step 1: μ = Fs / (mg)

Step 2: μ = 3 N / (15 kg × 10 ms&sup-2;) = 3 / 150

Step 3: μ = 0.02

Anti-lock Braking System (ABS)

The ABS uses sensors to detect when a wheel is about to lock; it rapidly releases and re-applies the brake many times a second, so the wheels keep rolling instead of skidding. Rolling grip (static friction) is stronger than sliding friction, so the vehicle stops in a shorter distance without sliding off course.

Uses of Rolling Friction

  • Wheels of cars, buses and cycles
  • Ball bearings in machines
  • Roller skates and skateboards
  • Moving heavy loads on rollers or trolleys

The relationship between load and friction can be identified by sliding a trolley carrying different loads with the help of a spring balance on different surfaces.

mcqs.q: Friction opposes motion between two bodies in contact because of:
mcqs.why: Friction arises from the roughness of the two surfaces in contact: their tiny irregularities lock into each other and oppose sliding, so friction opposes motion.

mcqs.q: Which statement is true for the limiting frictional force?
options: It is greater than rolling friction
It is greater than sliding friction
It is greater than kinetic friction
mcqs.why: The limiting (maximum static) friction is the largest of all: it is greater than rolling, sliding and kinetic friction, which is why starting a motion is harder than keeping it going.

mcqs.q: A block of mass 15 kg on a wet floor is pulled with a force of 3 N (spring balance). The coefficient of friction (F<sub>s</sub> = μmg) is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: μ = F<sub>s</sub> / (mg) = 3 / (15 × 10). Step 2: μ = 3 / 150. Step 3: μ = 0.02.

mcqs.q: The anti-lock braking system (ABS) prevents sliding because it:
options: keeps the wheels rolling instead of locking and skidding
increases the mass of the car
mcqs.why: ABS sensors detect a wheel about to lock and rapidly release and re-apply the brake many times a second. The wheels keep rolling, and rolling grip is stronger than sliding friction, so the vehicle stops sooner without skidding.

mcqs.q: Which of the following uses rolling friction?
mcqs.why: Ball bearings roll between the moving parts of a machine, replacing sliding friction with much smaller rolling friction. Wheels, roller skates and trolleys also use rolling friction.

mcqs.q: Rolling friction is ______ sliding friction.
mcqs.why: Rolling friction is much less than sliding friction. That is why wheels and ball bearings make it so much easier to move heavy objects.

mcqs.q: Friction is a force that:
options: opposes motion between surfaces in contact
mcqs.why: Friction always acts opposite to the motion (or attempted motion) between two surfaces in contact. It can be useful, as in walking, or wasteful, as in machine parts.

mcqs.q: In the formula F<sub>s</sub> = μmg, the symbol μ stands for:
mcqs.why: μ (mu) is the coefficient of friction between the two surfaces. It has no unit and depends on how rough the surfaces are — 0.02 for the wet slippery floor in the example.

mcqs.q: A cyclist must keep paddling (pedalling) continuously because:
options: friction and air resistance slow it down, so pedalling supplies force to balance them
mcqs.why: Without pedalling, friction and air resistance act as unbalanced forces and slow the bicycle (first law). Continuous pedalling provides the force needed to balance them and keep the speed steady.

mcqs.q: When an air-filled balloon is released and flies off, the principle involved is:
options: Newton's third law: air rushes out one way (action) and the balloon is pushed the opposite way (reaction)
mcqs.why: Air rushes out of the balloon in one direction (action) and the balloon is pushed in the opposite direction (reaction) — Newton's third law of motion. The balloon also loses mass as the air escapes.

lessons.title: Like and Unlike Parallel Forces; Addition of Forces
lessons.notes_html:
Like parallel forces act in the same direction. Unlike parallel forces act in opposite directions.

  • Resultant of two like parallel forces of 15 N each = 15 N + 15 N = 30 N in the direction of the forces.
  • Resultant of two unlike parallel forces of 10 N each along the same line = 10 N − 10 N = 0 N; the two forces cancel each other.

Head-to-Tail Rule

Draw the first force vector, then draw the next vector with its tail at the head of the previous one, and so on. The vector joining the tail of the first to the head of the last is the resultant. The rule can add any number of forces.

Worked Example

Three forces: 12 N along the x-axis, 8 N at 45° to the x-axis, and 8 N along the y-axis. Find the resultant and its direction.

Step 1: Fx = 12 + 8 cos 45° = 12 + 5.66 = 17.66 N

Step 2: Fy = 8 + 8 sin 45° = 8 + 5.66 = 13.66 N

Step 3: R = √(17.66² + 13.66²) = √(311.9 + 186.6) = √498.5 = 22.3 N

Step 4: Direction θ = tan&sup-1;(13.66 / 17.66) = tan&sup-1;(0.774) = 37.7° above the x-axis

mcqs.q: A pair of like parallel forces of 15 N each acts on a body. Their resultant is:
mcqs.why: Like parallel forces act in the same direction, so they simply add: R = 15 N + 15 N = 30 N in the direction of the forces.

mcqs.q: Two unlike parallel forces of 10 N each act along the same line. Their resultant is:
mcqs.why: Unlike parallel forces act in opposite directions, so the resultant is the difference: R = 10 N − 10 N = 0 N. The two forces cancel each other.

mcqs.q: Like parallel forces are forces that act:
mcqs.why: Parallel forces acting in the same direction are called like parallel forces. Those acting in opposite directions are unlike parallel forces.

mcqs.q: The head-to-tail rule can be used to add ______ forces.
mcqs.why: In the head-to-tail rule each new vector is drawn from the head of the previous one, so it works for two, three or any number of forces.

mcqs.q: In the head-to-tail rule, the resultant is the vector drawn from:
options: the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector
the head of the first to the tail of the last
mcqs.why: After placing all the vectors head-to-tail, the single vector from the tail of the first to the head of the last gives the resultant in magnitude and direction.

mcqs.q: Three forces: 12 N along x, 8 N at 45° to x, 8 N along y. The x-component of the resultant is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: F<sub>x</sub> = 12 + 8 cos 45°. Step 2: F<sub>x</sub> = 12 + 5.66 = 17.66 N. The y-force has no x-component.

mcqs.q: For the same three forces, the magnitude of the resultant is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: F<sub>x</sub> = 17.66 N, F<sub>y</sub> = 13.66 N. Step 2: R = √(17.66² + 13.66²) = √498.5. Step 3: R = 22.3 N.

mcqs.q: The direction of that resultant, measured from the x-axis, is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: tan θ = F<sub>y</sub> / F<sub>x</sub> = 13.66 / 17.66 = 0.774. Step 2: θ = tan&sup-1;(0.774) = 37.7° above the x-axis.

mcqs.q: Unlike parallel forces with different lines of action tend to produce:
mcqs.why: Two equal, opposite, parallel forces with different lines of action form a couple, which produces rotation without moving the body bodily.

mcqs.q: If two equal unlike parallel forces act on a body along the same line, the body:
mcqs.why: Equal unlike forces along the same line cancel exactly: the resultant is 10 − 10 = 0 N, so there is no net force on the body.

lessons.title: Resolution of a Force into Its Components
lessons.notes_html:
A force F acting at an angle θ to the horizontal is resolved into two perpendicular (rectangular) components:

Fx = F cos θ (horizontal component)

Fy = F sin θ (vertical component)

Conversely, a force can be determined from its rectangular components:

F = √(Fx² + Fy²),   θ = tan&sup-1;(Fy / Fx)

Worked Example 1

A gardener drives a lawnmower with a force of 80 N at 40° to the ground. Find its components.

Step 1: Horizontal component = 80 cos 40° = 80 × 0.766 = 61.3 N

Step 2: Vertical component = 80 sin 40° = 80 × 0.643 = 51.4 N

Worked Example 2

The horizontal and vertical components of a force are 4 N and 3 N. Find the force and its direction.

Step 1: F = √(4² + 3²) = √25 = 5 N

Step 2: θ = tan&sup-1;(3 / 4) = 36.9° above the horizontal

mcqs.q: A force of 15 N makes an angle of 60° with the horizontal. Its vertical component is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Vertical component = F sin θ = 15 × sin 60°. Step 2: = 15 × 0.866. Step 3: = 13 N.

mcqs.q: A force F at angle θ to the horizontal has horizontal component:
mcqs.why: The component along the direction making angle θ with the force uses the cosine: F<sub>x</sub> = F cos θ. The perpendicular component is F<sub>y</sub> = F sin θ.

mcqs.q: A gardener pushes a lawnmower with 80 N at 40° to the ground. The horizontal component is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: F<sub>x</sub> = F cos θ = 80 × cos 40°. Step 2: = 80 × 0.766. Step 3: = 61.3 N. This is the component that actually moves the mower forward.

mcqs.q: The vertical component of the gardener's 80 N force at 40° is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: F<sub>y</sub> = F sin θ = 80 × sin 40°. Step 2: = 80 × 0.643. Step 3: = 51.4 N.

mcqs.q: The horizontal and vertical components of a force are 4 N and 3 N. The magnitude of the force is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: F = √(F<sub>x</sub>² + F<sub>y</sub>²) = √(4² + 3²). Step 2: = √(16 + 9) = √25. Step 3: F = 5 N.

mcqs.q: The direction of that force (components 4 N and 3 N) is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: tan θ = F<sub>y</sub> / F<sub>x</sub> = 3 / 4 = 0.75. Step 2: θ = tan&sup-1;(0.75) = 36.9° above the horizontal.

mcqs.q: Resolution of a force means:
options: splitting a force into two perpendicular components
mcqs.why: Resolution is the reverse of addition: one force is replaced by two perpendicular (rectangular) components, F cos θ and F sin θ, which together have the same effect.

mcqs.q: If the components of a force are F<sub>x</sub> = 6 N and F<sub>y</sub> = 8 N, the force is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: F = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64). Step 2: = √100. Step 3: F = 10 N.

mcqs.q: A force acts vertically upward only. Its horizontal component is:
mcqs.why: A vertical force has θ = 90° to the horizontal, so F<sub>x</sub> = F cos 90° = F × 0 = 0. Its whole effect is in the vertical component.

mcqs.q: The two rectangular components of a force are ______ to each other.
mcqs.why: Rectangular components are taken along two directions at right angles (perpendicular) to each other — usually horizontal and vertical — so that Pythagoras' theorem can be applied.

lessons.title: Moment of Force (Torque) and Principle of Moments
lessons.notes_html:
The moment of force (torque) is the turning effect of a force:

Torque = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot (moment arm)

Its unit is the newton-metre (Nm). The turning effect of a force is used in the working of a bottle opener, spanner, door and window handles.

Principle of moments: for a body in equilibrium, the sum of anticlockwise moments about any point equals the sum of clockwise moments about that point.

Worked Example 1

A spanner of length 0.3 m produces a torque of 300 Nm. Find the force applied, and the length needed to produce 500 Nm with the same force.

Step 1: F = torque / length = 300 Nm / 0.3 m = 1000 N

Step 2: length = torque / F = 500 Nm / 1000 N = 0.5 m

Worked Example 2

A uniform metre rule is balanced at the 30 cm mark when a load of 0.80 N is hung at the zero mark. Find the weight of the rule.

Step 1: The centre of gravity of a uniform rule is at its middle, the 50 cm mark — 20 cm from the pivot.

Step 2: Load moment about the pivot = 0.80 N × 30 cm = 24 N cm

Step 3: W × 20 cm = 24 N cm, so W = 1.2 N

mcqs.q: The moment of force (torque) is equal to:
options: force × perpendicular distance from the pivot
mcqs.why: Torque = force × perpendicular distance of the force from the pivot (the moment arm). A larger force or a longer arm gives a larger turning effect.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of torque is:
mcqs.why: Torque = force (N) × distance (m), so its unit is the newton-metre, written Nm.

mcqs.q: A spanner of 0.3 m length produces a torque of 300 Nm. The force applied on it is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: F = torque / length. Step 2: F = 300 Nm / 0.3 m. Step 3: F = 1000 N.

mcqs.q: With the same force of 1000 N, the spanner length needed to produce a torque of 500 Nm is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: length = torque / F. Step 2: length = 500 Nm / 1000 N. Step 3: length = 0.5 m. A longer spanner gives more turning effect for the same force.

mcqs.q: The principle of moments states that for a body in equilibrium:
options: sum of anticlockwise moments = sum of clockwise moments about any point
mcqs.why: Principle of moments: when a body is in equilibrium, the total anticlockwise moment about any point equals the total clockwise moment about that point.

mcqs.q: A uniform metre rule is balanced at the 30 cm mark with a 0.80 N load at the zero mark. The weight of the rule is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Load moment = 0.80 × 30 = 24 N cm. Step 2: The rule's weight acts at 50 cm, i.e. 20 cm from the pivot. Step 3: W = 24 / 20 = 1.2 N.

mcqs.q: The centre of gravity of a uniform metre rule is at:
mcqs.why: A uniform rule has its mass spread evenly, so its centre of gravity is at its middle point — the 50 cm mark.

mcqs.q: A door is easiest to open when the handle is:
options: at the middle of the door
mcqs.why: Torque = force × distance from the pivot (hinges). Placing the handle far from the hinges makes the moment arm large, so a small force gives a big turning effect.

mcqs.q: If the force on a spanner is doubled and its length is halved, the torque becomes:
mcqs.why: Torque = F × d. Doubling F gives 2F and halving d gives d/2, so the new torque = 2F × d/2 = Fd — the same as before.

mcqs.q: A metre rod balanced on a pivot (a wedge) is an example used to verify:
mcqs.why: Balancing a metre rod on a wedge and matching the moments on both sides verifies the principle of moments: anticlockwise moments equal clockwise moments in equilibrium.

lessons.title: Centre of Mass, Centre of Gravity and Couple
lessons.notes_html:
Centre of mass is the point at which the whole mass of a body is considered to be concentrated.

Centre of gravity is the point at which the whole weight of a body is considered to act. In uniform gravity the two points coincide.

Finding the Centre of Gravity

Hang the body from different points in turn and mark the vertical (plumb-line) direction each time; the lines cross at the centre of gravity. For regular bodies it is found from symmetry or geometry.

The position of the centre of mass of regularly shaped objects (like a uniform rod or a sphere) is at their geometric centre.

Couple

A couple is a pair of equal, opposite and parallel forces with different lines of action that tends to rotate a body without moving it bodily. The steering wheel and bicycle pedals work by a couple.

Torque of a couple = force × moment arm (distance between the two forces)

Worked Example

A mechanic uses a double-arm spanner and applies 15 N at each end to produce a torque of 60 Nm. Find the moment arm; then find the force needed for 80 Nm.

Step 1: Moment arm = torque / F = 60 Nm / 15 N = 4 m

Step 2: F = torque / moment arm = 80 Nm / 4 m = 20 N at each end

mcqs.q: A pair of unlike parallel forces having different lines of action produces ______.
mcqs.why: Two equal, opposite parallel forces with different lines of action form a couple. A couple produces rotation (torque) without moving the body bodily.

mcqs.q: Centre of mass is the point at which:
options: the whole weight of the body acts
the whole mass of the body is considered to be concentrated
mcqs.why: The centre of mass is the point where the whole mass of the body may be taken to be concentrated. The centre of gravity is where the whole weight acts.

mcqs.q: Centre of gravity is the point at which:
options: the whole weight of the body is considered to act
mcqs.why: The centre of gravity is the point through which the whole weight of the body acts, wherever the body is placed. In uniform gravity it coincides with the centre of mass.

mcqs.q: The centre of gravity of an irregularly shaped object is found by:
options: hanging it from different points and marking the plumb-line directions; the lines cross at the centre of gravity
mcqs.why: Hang the object freely from one point and draw the vertical line from that point; repeat from other points. All the lines cross at one point — the centre of gravity.

mcqs.q: A couple consists of two forces that are:
options: equal, in the same direction, same line
equal, opposite and parallel, with different lines of action
mcqs.why: A couple is a pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces whose lines of action are different, so they produce pure rotation, e.g. turning a steering wheel.

mcqs.q: A mechanic applies 15 N at each end of a double-arm spanner and produces a torque of 60 Nm. The moment arm of the couple is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Torque of a couple = F × moment arm. Step 2: Moment arm = 60 Nm / 15 N. Step 3: Moment arm = 4 m (the book's worked example values).

mcqs.q: To produce a torque of 80 Nm with the same spanner (moment arm 4 m), the force at each end should be:
mcqs.why: Step 1: F = torque / moment arm. Step 2: F = 80 Nm / 4 m. Step 3: F = 20 N at each end.

mcqs.q: Which everyday action works by a couple?
mcqs.why: Both hands apply equal and opposite forces at opposite sides of the steering wheel — a couple — which rotates the wheel without pushing it sideways. Bicycle pedals work the same way.

mcqs.q: A couple tends to ______ a body.
options: move it in a straight line
rotate it without moving it bodily
mcqs.why: The two forces of a couple cancel for translation (resultant zero) but their moments add up, so the body only rotates.

mcqs.q: For a regularly shaped object such as a uniform sphere, the centre of mass is at:
mcqs.why: For bodies of regular shape and uniform density, symmetry places the centre of mass (and centre of gravity) at the geometric centre of the body.

lessons.title: Equilibrium and Stability
lessons.notes_html:
A body is in equilibrium when it has zero acceleration. Two conditions must hold:

  • First condition: the sum of all forces on the object is zero (net force = 0).
  • Second condition: the sum of all moments about any point is zero (net torque = 0).

Three States of Equilibrium

StateEffect of a slight tilt
StableCentre of gravity rises but its line of action still falls within the base; the body returns to its original position
UnstableThe line of action of the weight passes over (beyond) the point of contact/base; the body topples over
NeutralCentre of gravity remains at the same height; the body stays in its new position

Improving Stability

  • A Bunsen burner is made stable by increasing its base area — a wider base keeps the line of action of its weight within the base.
  • A tightrope walker carries a long pole to lower his centre of gravity.
  • The stability of a racing car is increased by lowering its centre of gravity.
  • The stability of an object can be improved by lowering the centre of mass and increasing the base area of the object — as in a balancing toy or a racing car.

mcqs.q: A body is in equilibrium when it has:
mcqs.why: Equilibrium means the net force and the net torque are both zero, so the body has zero acceleration — it stays at rest or keeps uniform motion without turning.

mcqs.q: A body is in stable equilibrium after a slight tilt if its centre of gravity:
options: remains above the point of contact, with its line of action within the base
mcqs.why: In stable equilibrium a slight tilt raises the centre of gravity, but the line of action of the weight still falls within the base, so the body returns to its original position.

mcqs.q: A body is in unstable equilibrium after a slight tilt if its centre of gravity:
options: remains above the point of contact
passes over the point of contact (beyond the base)
mcqs.why: In unstable equilibrium the tilt moves the line of action of the weight beyond the base (past the point of contact), so instead of returning, the body topples over.

mcqs.q: A body is in neutral equilibrium when its centre of gravity:
mcqs.why: In neutral equilibrium, displacement does not raise or lower the centre of gravity; it stays at the same height, so the body remains in its new position (like a ball on a flat surface).

mcqs.q: A Bunsen burner is made stable by:
mcqs.why: A wider base means the line of action of the weight stays within the base even when the burner is tilted a little, so increasing the base area makes it stable.

mcqs.q: A tightrope walker carries a long pole to:
mcqs.why: The long pole lowers the combined centre of gravity of the walker and also increases the moment of inertia, making balance on the rope much easier.

mcqs.q: The stability of a racing car is increased by:
mcqs.why: A low centre of gravity (with a wide base) keeps the line of action of the car's weight inside the base during fast turns, so the car remains stable.

mcqs.q: The two conditions necessary for an object to be in equilibrium are:
options: net force zero and net moment zero
mcqs.why: First condition: the sum of all forces is zero. Second condition: the sum of all moments about any point is zero. Both must hold for complete equilibrium.

mcqs.q: A simple balanced system supported by one pivot only is in equilibrium when:
options: the moments on the two sides are equal and opposite
mcqs.why: For a beam balanced on one pivot, equilibrium requires the clockwise moments to equal the anticlockwise moments about the pivot (principle of moments).

mcqs.q: The stability of an object can be improved by:
options: raising its centre of mass and narrowing its base
lowering its centre of mass and increasing its base area
mcqs.why: Lower centre of mass plus a wider base area is the recipe for stability — used in the balancing toy, the Bunsen burner and the racing car.

lessons.title: Elasticity and Hooke's Law
lessons.notes_html:
A force can change the shape and size of a body. If the material recovers its original dimensions when the external force is removed, the deformation is called elastic deformation.

Hooke's law: within the elastic limit, the extension of a spring is directly proportional to the applied force:

F = kx

where k is the spring constant. Its unit is Nm&sup-1; (newton per metre). If a spring stretches easily, its spring constant has a small value — a small force produces a large extension.

Of rubber, glass, steel and wood, steel is the most elastic: it returns fully to its shape and has the highest modulus of elasticity. Rubber stretches more, but is less elastic in the physics sense.

Worked Example

Calculate the spring constant of a spring which extends by 3.5 cm when a load of 14 N is hung from its end.

Step 1: Convert the extension to metres: x = 3.5 cm = 0.035 m

Step 2: k = F / x = 14 N / 0.035 m

Step 3: k = 400 Nm&sup-1;

Springs in brakes and clutches are used to restore the original position.

mcqs.q: If a material recovers its original dimensions when an external force is removed, this deformation is known as ______ deformation.
mcqs.why: Elastic deformation is temporary: the material returns to its original size and shape when the force is removed. Permanent (plastic) deformation does not recover.

mcqs.q: Which of the following materials is more elastic?
mcqs.why: Steel is the most elastic of these: it returns fully to its shape and has the highest modulus of elasticity. Rubber stretches much more, but stretching a lot is not the same as being more elastic in physics.

mcqs.q: If a spring stretches easily, then its spring constant has ______.
mcqs.why: Spring constant k = F / x. If a small force makes a large extension, k is small. A stiff spring that barely stretches has a large k.

mcqs.q: What is the unit of the spring constant?
mcqs.why: k = F / x, so its unit is newtons per metre: Nm&sup-1;. Nm is the unit of torque and Nm&sup-2; (pascal) is the unit of pressure.

mcqs.q: Hooke's law states that, within the elastic limit:
options: extension is inversely proportional to force
extension is directly proportional to the applied force
mcqs.why: Hooke's law: F = kx. Within the elastic limit the extension x grows in direct proportion to the applied force F, so the extension–load graph is a straight line.
