mcqs.q: Calculate the spring constant for a spring which extends by 3.5 cm when a load of 14 N is hung from it.
mcqs.why: Step 1: x = 3.5 cm = 0.035 m. Step 2: k = F / x = 14 N / 0.035 m. Step 3: k = 400 Nm&sup-1;. The extension must be in metres for k in Nm&sup-1;.

mcqs.q: The springs in brakes and clutches are used:
mcqs.why: In brakes and clutches the springs return the parts to their original position when the pedal or lever is released — they work by elastic recovery.

mcqs.q: In the formula F = kx, the constant k is called:
mcqs.why: k is the spring constant: the force needed to produce unit extension of the spring. It is measured in Nm&sup-1; and depends on the spring's material and construction.

mcqs.q: A spring with k = 200 Nm&sup-1; is loaded with 10 N. Its extension is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: x = F / k. Step 2: x = 10 N / 200 Nm&sup-1;. Step 3: x = 0.05 m (5 cm).

mcqs.q: A force can change the ______ of a body besides changing its motion.
mcqs.why: Besides making objects speed up, slow down, start moving, stop or change direction, a force also has another effect: it can change the shape and size of a body, as when a spring is stretched.

lessons.title: Extension–Load Graph, Elastic Limit and Limit of Proportionality
lessons.notes_html:
When loads are added to a spring and the extension is measured, the extension–load graph is a straight line through the origin while Hooke's law holds.

Book Experiment (Table 5.3)

Load (N)02468101214
Extension (mm)0153045607590100

The graph is straight up to 12 N (extension rises 15 mm for every 2 N, i.e. 7.5 mm per N). The last point (14 N, 100 mm) falls below the line, showing the spring is past its elastic limit there.

  • Extension when the load is 3 N = 3 × 7.5 mm = 22.5 mm
  • Load which produces an extension of 40 mm = 40 / 7.5 = 5.33 N

Elastic limit: the greatest force (or extension) up to which the spring returns to its original length when the force is removed. Beyond the elastic limit the spring is permanently deformed and Hooke's law no longer holds.

Second Book Experiment (Table 5.4)

Extensions (length minus the 80 cm unstretched length) are 0, 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 13 cm for loads 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 N. The graph is straight (3 cm for every 2 N) and bends after 10 N.

  • Limit of proportionality: at load 10 N (extension 12 cm)
  • Spring constant in the proportional region: k = 2 N / 0.03 m = 66.7 Nm&sup-1;
  • Hooke's law is applicable up to a maximum force of 10 N

A spring obeys Hooke's law for the earlier extensions; in Fig. 5.12 the graph stays straight up to about 1.6 N and then bends — after the addition of about 1.6 N weight the spring is damaged (in another graph, Fig. 5.14, the elastic limit L lies at a force of about 8 N, extension about 7.4 cm).

mcqs.q: In the book's spring experiment, the extension rises by 15 mm for every 2 N of load. The extension produced by a load of 3 N is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Rate = 15 mm / 2 N = 7.5 mm per N. Step 2: Extension at 3 N = 3 × 7.5 mm = 22.5 mm. This uses the straight (proportional) part of the graph.

mcqs.q: In the same experiment, the load which produces an extension of 40 mm is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Extension per newton = 7.5 mm/N. Step 2: Load = 40 mm / 7.5 mm per N = 5.33 N.

mcqs.q: The elastic limit of a spring is:
options: the point where the spring breaks
the greatest force up to which the spring returns to its original length when the force is removed
the natural length of the spring
mcqs.why: Up to the elastic limit the deformation is elastic — remove the force and the spring recovers fully. Beyond it the spring is permanently deformed and Hooke's law no longer holds.

mcqs.q: In the experiment of Table 5.3 the last point (14 N, 100 mm) falls below the straight line. This shows that:
options: the spring became stiffer in proportion
the spring is past its elastic limit there
mcqs.why: While Hooke's law holds, points lie on a straight line through the origin. The 14 N point bending away from the line shows the spring has passed its elastic limit and is permanently stretched.

mcqs.q: In the second experiment (Table 5.4), the limit of proportionality is at a load of:
mcqs.why: Extensions grow by 3 cm for every 2 N up to 10 N (extension 12 cm); after 10 N the graph bends. So the limit of proportionality — the end of the straight part — is at 10 N.

mcqs.q: The spring constant from the proportional region of Table 5.4 (2 N produces 3 cm extension) is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Convert: 3 cm = 0.03 m. Step 2: k = F / x = 2 N / 0.03 m. Step 3: k = 66.7 Nm&sup-1;.

mcqs.q: In Table 5.4, Hooke's law is applicable up to a maximum force of:
mcqs.why: Hooke's law holds only while the graph is straight, that is up to the limit of proportionality at 10 N. Beyond 10 N the extension is no longer proportional to the load.

mcqs.q: A spring obeys Hooke's law for the earlier extensions, and the graph of Fig. 5.12 bends after about 1.6 N. This means the spring is damaged after the addition of about:
mcqs.why: In Fig. 5.12 the extension–weight graph is a straight line up to about 1.6 N; beyond that it bends away, so the spring no longer obeys Hooke's law and is damaged.

mcqs.q: On an extension–load graph, the straight-line portion through the origin shows the region where:
options: extension is directly proportional to load (Hooke's law holds)
mcqs.why: A straight line through the origin means extension ∝ load — exactly Hooke's law. The slope of this line also gives the extension per unit load.

mcqs.q: Beyond the elastic limit, a spring:
options: is permanently deformed and does not return to its original length
mcqs.why: Past the elastic limit the spring's internal structure is changed; it keeps a permanent stretch even after the load is removed, and Hooke's law no longer applies.

lessons.title: Pressure in Solids
lessons.notes_html:
Pressure is the force acting per unit area:

P = F / A

Its SI unit is the pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 Nm&sup-2;. Bar and atmosphere are also units of pressure; the newton is not — it is the unit of force.

For the same force, pressure is greater on a smaller area: pressure is inversely proportional to area.

Worked Example: The Thumbtack

A boy presses a thumbtack into wood with a force of 20 N. The head has area 1 cm² and the tip has area 0.01 cm².

Step 1: Pressure on the head = F / A = 20 N / 1 cm² = 20 N/cm²

Step 2: Pressure of the tip on the wood = F / A = 20 N / 0.01 cm² = 2000 N/cm²

Step 3: Conclusion — for the same force, the smaller area gives far greater pressure. That is why the sharp tip pierces the wood while the wide head does not hurt the thumb much.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is not a unit of pressure?
mcqs.why: Pascal, bar and atmosphere are all units of pressure. The newton is the unit of force — pressure is force per unit area, so it cannot be measured in newtons alone.

mcqs.q: Pressure is defined as:
options: force per unit area (P = F / A)
mcqs.why: Pressure is the force acting per unit area: P = F / A. Its SI unit is the pascal, where 1 Pa = 1 Nm&sup-2;.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of pressure is:
mcqs.why: The SI unit of pressure is the pascal (Pa): 1 Pa = 1 Nm&sup-2;, i.e. a force of one newton spread over one square metre.

mcqs.q: A metal block applies a force of 20 N on an area of 5 cm². The pressure applied by the block is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: P = F / A. Step 2: P = 20 N / 5 cm². Step 3: P = 4 N/cm².

mcqs.q: A boy presses a thumbtack with a force of 20 N. The head area is 1 cm². The pressure on the head is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: P = F / A = 20 N / 1 cm². Step 2: P = 20 N/cm². This moderate pressure is spread over the thumb, so it does not hurt much.

mcqs.q: The tip of the same thumbtack has area 0.01 cm². The pressure of the tip on the wood is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: P = F / A = 20 N / 0.01 cm². Step 2: P = 2000 N/cm². The same force on a 100-times smaller area gives 100 times more pressure.

mcqs.q: The thumbtack example shows that, for the same force, pressure is:
mcqs.why: P = F / A: with F fixed, halving the area doubles the pressure. The sharp tip pierces the wood precisely because its tiny area makes the pressure huge.

mcqs.q: A force of 100 N acts on an area of 2 m². The pressure is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: P = F / A = 100 N / 2 m². Step 2: P = 50 Pa (50 Nm&sup-2;).

mcqs.q: A sharp knife cuts more easily than a blunt one because:
options: its edge has a very small area, so the same force gives a much greater pressure
mcqs.why: Pressure = force / area. The sharp edge concentrates the force onto a tiny area, producing a very large pressure that cuts through the material.

mcqs.q: If the area over which a force acts is doubled (same force), the pressure becomes:
mcqs.why: P = F / A. With F unchanged and A doubled, P is halved. This is why wide foundations and broad straps reduce pressure.

lessons.title: Pressure in Liquids and Hydraulic Machines
lessons.notes_html:
The pressure at a depth h in a liquid is:

P = ρgh

As a diver goes deeper, the weight of the water column above increases, so the pressure increases with depth. In a container with spouts at different heights, the jet from the bottom spout goes farthest because the pressure there is greatest.

Hydraulic System (Pascal's Law)

Pressure applied to a fluid is transmitted equally through it. Fig. 5.15 shows a hydraulic system with a small piston of area 0.005 m² and a large piston of area 0.1 m². A force of 20 N is applied to the small piston.

Step 1: Pressure transmitted = P = F / A = 20 N / 0.005 m² = 4000 Pa

Step 2: Force at the large piston = P × A = 4000 Pa × 0.1 m² = 400 N

Step 3: The fluid is incompressible, so the volume moved is the same on both sides: dsmall / dlarge = 0.1 / 0.005 = 20. The small piston travels 20 times farther than the large piston, while the large piston lifts 20 times the force. The work done on both sides is the same.

mcqs.q: A container has three spouts at different heights, filled with water. The jet from the bottom spout goes farthest because:
options: more water is available at the bottom
density of water is different at different places
mcqs.why: Liquid pressure P = ρgh grows with depth. The bottom spout is deepest, so the water pressure there is greatest and the jet shoots out fastest and farthest.

mcqs.q: Pressure in a liquid at depth h is given by:
mcqs.why: The pressure at a depth h in a liquid of density ρ is P = ρgh: it comes from the weight of the liquid column above that point.

mcqs.q: Why does pressure increase as divers go deeper into the sea?
options: The water becomes denser with depth
The weight of the water column above the diver increases with depth
mcqs.why: P = ρgh. Going deeper increases h, the height of the water column pressing down, so the pressure on the diver increases.

mcqs.q: In a hydraulic system, a force of 20 N on a small piston of area 0.005 m² creates a pressure in the fluid of:
mcqs.why: Step 1: P = F / A = 20 N / 0.005 m². Step 2: P = 4000 Pa. By Pascal's law this pressure is transmitted equally through the fluid.

mcqs.q: The large piston of the same system has area 0.1 m². The force it exerts is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: F = P × A. Step 2: F = 4000 Pa × 0.1 m². Step 3: F = 400 N — twenty times the input force, because the area is twenty times bigger.

mcqs.q: In the hydraulic system, if the large piston rises by 1 cm, the small piston must move:
mcqs.why: The fluid is incompressible, so the volume moved is equal on both sides: A<sub>small</sub> × d<sub>small</sub> = A<sub>large</sub> × d<sub>large</sub>. The area ratio is 20, so the small piston travels 20 × 1 cm = 20 cm.

mcqs.q: Pascal's law is the basis of hydraulic machines. It states that pressure applied to a fluid is:
options: transmitted equally in all directions through the fluid
mcqs.why: Pascal's law: pressure applied anywhere to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally and undiminished throughout the fluid — this is what lets a small force on a small piston lift a heavy load on a large piston.

mcqs.q: The work done by the small piston and the work done by the large piston in a hydraulic machine are:
options: different; the large side does more
mcqs.why: Force is multiplied (20 N becomes 400 N) but distance is divided by the same factor (the small piston moves 20 times farther), so work = force × distance is the same on both sides — energy is conserved.

mcqs.q: A hydraulic press has pistons of area 0.02 m² and 0.5 m². A force of 10 N on the small piston will lift a load of:
mcqs.why: Step 1: P = 10 N / 0.02 m² = 500 Pa. Step 2: F = P × A = 500 × 0.5. Step 3: F = 250 N.

mcqs.q: Pressure at a point in a liquid depends on:
options: the shape of the container only
the depth and the density of the liquid
the total volume of liquid only
mcqs.why: From P = ρgh, liquid pressure depends on the depth h below the surface and the density ρ of the liquid (and g) — not on the shape of the container or the total volume.

lessons.title: Newton's Law of Gravitation and the Gravitational Field
lessons.notes_html:
Newton's law of gravitation: every two masses in the universe attract each other with a force that is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them:

F = G m1m2 / r²

G is the universal gravitational constant:

G = 6.673 × 10&sup-1;¹ Nm² kg&sup-2;

The gravitational forces are consistent with Newton's third law: the two masses pull each other with equal and opposite forces.

Characteristics of Gravitational Force

  • It is always attractive, never repulsive.
  • It acts between any two masses anywhere in the universe.
  • It is independent of the medium between the masses.
  • It follows the inverse-square law (weakens as 1 / r²).

We do not feel the gravitational attraction of objects around us because their masses are very small, so the force F = G m1m2 / r² is extremely tiny compared with the Earth's pull.

Gravitational Field

A gravitational field is the region around a mass in which another mass feels a gravitational force — for example, the region around the Earth, where a released ball is pulled towards it. The Earth's gravitational field is directed towards the Earth.

Gravitational field strength at a point is the gravitational force per unit mass at that point:

g = F / m

Its unit is N/kg (the same as ms&sup-2;). A field force is a force that acts at a distance through a field, without direct contact — for example, the gravitational force.

Worked Example

Find the gravitational force between Urwa (mass 60 kg) and Ayesha (mass 70 kg) standing 50 m apart.

Step 1: F = G m1m2 / r² = 6.673 × 10&sup-1;¹ × 60 × 70 / 50²

Step 2: F = 6.673 × 10&sup-1;¹ × 4200 / 2500 = 6.673 × 10&sup-1;¹ × 1.68

Step 3: F = 1.12 × 10&sup-1;&sup0; N — far too small to feel

mcqs.q: The motion of a falling ball towards the Earth is due to the ______.
mcqs.why: The Earth's gravitational pull attracts the ball and gives it the acceleration due to gravity (g), so the falling motion is due to the gravitational force.

mcqs.q: Newton's law of gravitation holds between every two objects:
mcqs.why: It is a universal law: any two masses anywhere in the universe attract each other with F = G m<sub>1</sub>m<sub>2</sub> / r².

mcqs.q: The numerical value of G is:
mcqs.why: The universal gravitational constant is G = 6.673 × 10&sup-1;¹ Nm² kg&sup-2;. Its very small value is why gravity between everyday objects is unnoticeable.

mcqs.q: The gravitational field of the Earth is directed:
mcqs.why: A gravitational field points towards the mass producing it: near the Earth every mass is pulled towards the Earth, so the field is directed towards the Earth.

mcqs.q: ______ was the first scientist who gave the concept of gravitation.
mcqs.why: Isaac Newton first gave the law of universal gravitation, explaining that the same force that pulls an apple down also holds the Moon and planets in their orbits.

mcqs.q: According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the force is proportional to:
mcqs.why: F = G m<sub>1</sub>m<sub>2</sub> / r²: the force grows with the product of the masses and falls with the square of the distance, so it is proportional to both m<sub>1</sub>m<sub>2</sub> and 1 / r².

mcqs.q: Gravitational force is always ______.
mcqs.why: Gravity only pulls masses together; it is always attractive and never repulsive, unlike electric and magnetic forces which can also repel.

mcqs.q: The numerical value of ______ remains constant everywhere.
mcqs.why: G, the universal gravitational constant, has the same value everywhere in the universe. The value of g (and so weight W) changes from place to place.

mcqs.q: Gravitational force is ______ of the medium between the objects.
mcqs.why: Gravity acts through empty space and through any medium unchanged; it does not depend on what lies between the two masses.

mcqs.q: Near the Earth's surface, g is equal to:
mcqs.why: Near Earth's surface the acceleration due to gravity is g = 10 ms&sup-2; in this book. The value 1.6 ms&sup-2; is the Moon's g.

mcqs.q: Newton's law of gravitation is consistent with Newton's ______ law of motion.
mcqs.why: The law works together with all three laws of motion; in particular the two masses pull each other with equal and opposite forces, exactly as the third law requires.

mcqs.q: We do not feel the gravitational attraction of the objects around us because:
options: gravity does not act on small objects
their masses are very small, so the force is extremely tiny compared with the Earth's pull
mcqs.why: F = G m<sub>1</sub>m<sub>2</sub> / r² with ordinary masses gives a force like 1.12 × 10&sup-1;&sup0; N — extremely tiny next to the Earth's pull, so we cannot feel it.

mcqs.q: A gravitational field is:
options: the region around a mass in which another mass feels a gravitational force
mcqs.why: A gravitational field is the region around a mass where another mass experiences a gravitational force, e.g. the region around the Earth in which a released ball is pulled down.

mcqs.q: Gravitational field strength at a point is defined as:
options: gravitational force per unit mass, g = F / m
mcqs.why: Field strength g = F / m is the force acting on each kilogram placed at that point. Its unit is N/kg, the same as ms&sup-2;.

mcqs.q: The gravitational force between Urwa (60 kg) and Ayesha (70 kg) standing 50 m apart is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: F = G m<sub>1</sub>m<sub>2</sub> / r² = 6.673 × 10&sup-1;¹ × 60 × 70 / 2500. Step 2: = 6.673 × 10&sup-1;¹ × 1.68. Step 3: F = 1.12 × 10&sup-1;&sup0; N.

lessons.title: Mass of the Earth and Variation of g
lessons.notes_html:
Combining Newton's law of gravitation with W = mg gives the acceleration due to gravity at the Earth's surface:

g = GM / R²

so the mass of the Earth can be calculated as:

M = gR² / G

Worked Example 1: Mass of the Earth

Step 1: M = gR² / G = 10 × (6.4 × 10&sup6;)² / (6.673 × 10&sup-1;¹)

Step 2: M = 10 × 4.096 × 10¹³ / (6.673 × 10&sup-1;¹)

Step 3: M = 6.14 × 10²&sup4; kg (about 6.0 × 10²&sup4; kg)

Value of g at Different Places

  • On the surface: g = GME / RE²
  • At the centre of the Earth: g = 0 — the mass pulls equally in all directions, so the net force is zero.
  • At a distance 2RE from the centre: g = GME / (2RE)² = gsurface / 4.

Worked Example 2

A planet has 4 times Earth's mass and 2 times Earth's radius. Find g on the planet (g on Earth = 10 ms&sup-2;).

Step 1: gplanet = G(4M) / (2R)² = 4GM / 4R²

Step 2: gplanet = GM / R² = gEarth

Step 3: gplanet = 10 ms&sup-2;

Note: the formula g = GM / r² applies outside the Earth. For a point inside the Earth, only the mass within that radius pulls, so at half the radius g becomes g/2, not 4g.

mcqs.q: The mass of the Earth is:
mcqs.why: From M = gR² / G the mass of the Earth comes out to about 6.0 × 10²&sup4; kg (the book's calculation gives 6.14 × 10²&sup4; kg).

mcqs.q: The mass of the Earth is calculated from Newton's law of gravitation using:
mcqs.why: From g = GM / R², rearranging gives M = gR² / G. Putting g = 10 ms&sup-2;, R = 6.4 × 10&sup6; m and G = 6.673 × 10&sup-1;¹ gives about 6 × 10²&sup4; kg.

mcqs.q: The acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the Earth is:
mcqs.why: Setting the weight mg equal to the gravitational force GMm / R² and cancelling m gives g = GM<sub>E</sub> / R<sub>E</sub>² at the surface.

mcqs.q: The value of g at the centre of the Earth is:
mcqs.why: At the centre the surrounding mass pulls equally in all directions, so the net gravitational force — and hence g — is zero.

mcqs.q: At a distance twice the Earth's radius from its centre, g becomes:
mcqs.why: Step 1: g = GM / (2R)² = GM / 4R². Step 2: This is one quarter of the surface value g = GM / R², because g follows the inverse-square law.

mcqs.q: A planet has 4 times Earth's mass and 2 times Earth's radius. The value of g on the planet (Earth's g = 10 ms&sup-2;) is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: g<sub>planet</sub> = G(4M) / (2R)² = 4GM / 4R². Step 2: = GM / R² = g<sub>Earth</sub>. Step 3: g<sub>planet</sub> = 10 ms&sup-2;. The factors of 4 cancel.

mcqs.q: Your weight decreases as you go up to a high altitude because:
options: g = GM / r² becomes smaller as r increases
mcqs.why: Weight W = mg, and g = GM / r² where r is the distance from Earth's centre. Higher up, r is larger, so g — and therefore weight — is smaller, while mass stays the same.

mcqs.q: The weight of an object does not remain the same everywhere on Earth because:
options: g is slightly greater at the poles than at the equator and decreases with height
mcqs.why: Weight W = mg follows g. Since g varies — a little more at the poles than at the equator, and less at greater heights — the weight of the same object changes from place to place.

mcqs.q: Doubling the distance from the centre of the Earth makes g:
mcqs.why: g follows the inverse-square law, g ∝ 1 / r². Doubling r divides g by 2² = 4, making it one quarter.

mcqs.q: Which quantity stays the same when an object is taken from the Earth to a high mountain?
options: The value of g acting on it
The reading of a spring balance
mcqs.why: Mass is the quantity of matter in the object and does not depend on place. Weight, g and the spring-balance reading all decrease slightly at height.

lessons.title: Weight and Its Measurement
lessons.notes_html:
Weight is the gravitational force with which the Earth attracts a body (the force on an object due to gravitation):

W = mg

Weight is a force, so its unit is the newton (N). It is measured with a spring balance. A bathroom scale measures the force pressing on it but is calibrated to display mass in kilograms.

Worked Example 1

The weight of Rani is 450 N at the surface of the Earth. Find her mass.

Step 1: m = W / g

Step 2: m = 450 N / 10 ms&sup-2;

Step 3: m = 45 kg

Worked Example 2

The weight of Naveera is 700 N on Earth. What will her weight be on the Moon?

Step 1: The Moon's g is about one-sixth of the Earth's g.

Step 2: Wmoon = 700 N / 6 = 116.7 N (about 117 N)

mcqs.q: A spring balance is used to measure ______.
mcqs.why: A spring balance measures the pull of gravity on a body — its weight — in newtons. Mass is measured with a beam (physical) balance in kilograms.

mcqs.q: Your weight as measured on Earth will be ______ on the Moon.
mcqs.why: The Moon's g is about one-sixth of the Earth's g, so W = mg gives about one-sixth the weight on the Moon. The mass remains unchanged.

mcqs.q: Weight is defined as:
options: the quantity of matter in a body
the gravitational force with which the Earth attracts a body, W = mg
mcqs.why: Weight is the force of gravity on a body: W = mg. That is why its unit is the newton and why it changes where g changes.

mcqs.q: The unit of weight is the newton because weight is a:
mcqs.why: Weight is the Earth's gravitational pull on the body — a force. The SI unit of force is the newton, so weight is measured in newtons.

mcqs.q: The weight of Rani is 450 N on Earth. Her mass is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: m = W / g. Step 2: m = 450 N / 10 ms&sup-2;. Step 3: m = 45 kg.

mcqs.q: The weight of Naveera is 700 N on Earth. Her weight on the Moon will be about:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Moon's g ≈ Earth's g / 6. Step 2: W<sub>moon</sub> = 700 N / 6 = 116.7 N ≈ 117 N.

mcqs.q: If you step on a scale and it gives a reading of 55 kg, the quantity it shows is:
options: mass — the scale measures the force but is calibrated to display mass
mcqs.why: A bathroom scale actually responds to the force (weight) pressing on it, but its dial is calibrated in kilograms, so the 55 kg reading is your mass. Your weight is W = 55 × 10 = 550 N.

mcqs.q: An object of mass 45 kg has a weight on Earth (g = 10 ms&sup-2;) of:
mcqs.why: Step 1: W = mg. Step 2: W = 45 kg × 10 ms&sup-2;. Step 3: W = 450 N.

mcqs.q: Weight depends on mass and on:
options: the value of g at that place
mcqs.why: W = mg: for a fixed mass, the weight follows the local value of g, which varies with place, height and planet.

mcqs.q: The weight of a body at the centre of the Earth would be:
options: the same as on the surface
mcqs.why: At the centre g = 0 (the mass pulls equally in all directions), so W = mg = m × 0 = 0. The body would be weightless there, though its mass is unchanged.

lessons.title: Artificial Satellites and Orbital Motion
lessons.notes_html:
A satellite stays in orbit when the gravitational force provides exactly the centripetal force for its circular motion. For a satellite of mass m at altitude h:

mv² / (R + h) = GMm / (R + h)²

which gives the orbital speed:

v = √(GM / (R + h))

The orbital speed does not contain the satellite's own mass, so it is independent of the mass of the satellite. Artificial satellites are put into orbits by rockets.

Critical velocity is the minimum horizontal velocity needed to place a satellite in a stable circular orbit around the Earth:

vc = √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s for Earth

Types of Orbit

  • Low Earth Orbit (LEO)
  • Medium Earth Orbit (MEO)
  • Geostationary / Geosynchronous Orbit (GEO)
  • Polar Orbit

Orbits are characterised by their altitude, orbital period, inclination (tilt of the orbital plane) and shape (circular or elliptical — eccentricity).

A communication satellite is placed in orbit (usually geostationary) to relay radio, television, telephone and internet signals between distant places on Earth. It completes one revolution in 24 hours, matching the Earth's rotation. The Moon is a natural satellite of the Earth.

Natural vs Artificial Satellites

Natural satelliteArtificial satellite
Formed by nature; orbits a planet by itself (e.g. the Moon)Man-made; launched by a rocket and placed in orbit for a purpose such as communication, weather watch or navigation

Worked Example

Calculate the speed of a satellite orbiting at an altitude of 400 km above the Earth's surface (R = 6.4 × 10&sup6; m, g = 10 ms&sup-2;).

Step 1: v = √(gR² / (R + h)) = √(10 × (6.4 × 10&sup6;)² / (6.8 × 10&sup6;))

Step 2: v = √(6.02 × 10&sup7;)

Step 3: v = 7760 ms&sup-1; (about 7.8 km/s)

mcqs.q: ______ is a natural satellite.
mcqs.why: The Moon is Earth's natural satellite — it was formed by nature and orbits the Earth by itself. Earth, Jupiter and Mars are planets.

mcqs.q: A communication (geostationary) satellite completes one revolution around the Earth in ______ hours.
mcqs.why: A geostationary communication satellite takes 24 hours for one revolution, exactly matching the Earth's rotation, so it stays over the same place.

mcqs.q: The velocity of a satellite is ______ of its mass.
mcqs.why: In v = √(GM / (R + h)) the satellite's own mass m cancels out, so the orbital velocity does not depend on the mass of the satellite.

mcqs.q: ______ are used to put satellites into orbits.
mcqs.why: Only rockets can carry a satellite high above the atmosphere and give it the huge horizontal speed (about 7.9 km/s) needed to stay in orbit.

mcqs.q: The critical velocity (v<sub>c</sub>) is given by:
mcqs.why: For a close orbit, v<sub>c</sub> = √(gR). For Earth this is about 7.9 km/s — the minimum horizontal velocity for a stable circular orbit.

mcqs.q: The speed of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius (R + h) is:
mcqs.why: Gravity supplies the centripetal force: mv² / (R + h) = GMm / (R + h)². Cancelling m and one factor (R + h) gives v² = GM / (R + h), so v = √(GM / (R + h)).

mcqs.q: The speed of a satellite orbiting 400 km above the Earth (R = 6.4 × 10&sup6; m) is about:
mcqs.why: Step 1: v = √(gR² / (R + h)) = √(10 × (6.4 × 10&sup6;)² / 6.8 × 10&sup6;). Step 2: = √(6.02 × 10&sup7;). Step 3: v = 7760 ms&sup-1; ≈ 7.8 km/s.

mcqs.q: A communication satellite is a satellite placed in orbit to:
options: relay radio, television, telephone and internet signals between distant places
mcqs.why: Communication satellites — usually in geostationary orbit — receive signals from one part of the Earth and relay them to distant places for TV, telephone and internet services.

mcqs.q: Orbits are characterised by which parameters?
options: Colour and size of the satellite
Altitude, orbital period, inclination and shape
mcqs.why: An orbit is described by its altitude above Earth, its orbital period, the inclination (tilt) of its plane, and its shape — circular or elliptical (eccentricity).

mcqs.q: Critical velocity is:
options: the velocity of a falling ball
the minimum horizontal velocity needed to place a satellite in a stable circular orbit
mcqs.why: Critical velocity v<sub>c</sub> = √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s for Earth: below this speed a projected body falls back instead of settling into a stable circular orbit.

lessons.title: Kinetic Molecular Model and the States of Matter
lessons.notes_html:
Matter is made up of tiny particles called atoms and molecules. The kinetic molecular model explains matter by the motion of its particles — it is called kinetic because the particles of all matter are always moving.

The Three States of Matter

StateParticlesProperties
SolidClosely packed in fixed positions; only vibrate about their mean positionsFixed shape, fixed volume, incompressible, high density, cannot be poured
LiquidFree to move within the materialFixed volume but takes the shape of its container
GasWidely separated; move freely at high speedNo fixed shape or volume
  • Molecules are most closely packed in a solid and widely separated in a gas.
  • Molecules have minimum kinetic energy in a solid and move freely at high speed in a gas.
  • Solids (and liquids) are highly incompressible.

Why We Can Walk Through Air but Not Through a Wall

In air the molecules are far apart with very weak forces between them, so we push through easily. In water the molecules are closer but still free to move past one another, so we can swim through. In a solid wall the molecules are tightly packed in fixed positions with strong forces, so we cannot pass through.

A burning candle shows all three states together: solid wax, melted liquid wax, and gas (wax vapour in the flame).

mcqs.q: An object with particles close together and vibrating describes a ______.
mcqs.why: In a solid the particles are closely packed in fixed positions and can only vibrate about their mean positions — exactly the description given.

mcqs.q: A burning candle is an example of ______ state(s) of matter.
mcqs.why: A burning candle has solid wax, melted liquid wax around the wick, and gas (wax vapour) in the flame — all three states of matter at the same time.

mcqs.q: A solid can ______.
options: take the shape of its container
mcqs.why: A solid has a fixed shape and a fixed volume because its particles are locked in fixed positions. Taking the container's shape is a property of liquids, and free movement of gases.

mcqs.q: 'The particles are free to move within the material; it has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container' — this describes:
mcqs.why: A liquid keeps a fixed volume but flows into the shape of its container because its particles can move within the material while staying close together.

mcqs.q: In a solid, the particles:
options: are closely packed in fixed positions and only vibrate about their mean positions
mcqs.why: Solid particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces; their only motion is vibration about their mean positions, which gives the solid its fixed shape and volume.

mcqs.q: Any two properties of a solid are:
options: easily compressed and can be poured
mcqs.why: A solid has a fixed shape and a fixed volume; it is also incompressible, has high density and cannot be poured — any two of these are correct properties.

mcqs.q: The kinetic model of matter is called 'kinetic' because:
options: it explains matter by the motion (kinetic energy) of its particles, which are always moving
mcqs.why: 'Kinetic' refers to motion: the model explains the properties of matter through the constant motion and kinetic energy of its particles.

mcqs.q: Molecules are widely separated in which state of matter?
mcqs.why: In a gas the molecules are widely separated with large empty spaces between them, which is why a gas can be compressed easily and fills its container.

mcqs.q: Molecules are most closely packed, and have minimum kinetic energy, in:
mcqs.why: Solid particles are packed most closely and only vibrate in place, so their kinetic energy is the minimum of the three states. Gas particles have the most kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: We can walk through air and swim through water but cannot walk through a solid wall because:
options: air molecules are far apart and water molecules can move aside, but a solid's molecules are tightly packed with strong forces
air and water have no molecules
solids have no spaces at all in any sense
mcqs.why: In air the molecules are far apart with weak forces, and in water they can slide past one another, so we pass through. In a solid wall the molecules are tightly packed in fixed positions with strong forces, blocking our way.

lessons.title: Kinetic Theory of Gases
lessons.notes_html:
According to the kinetic molecular theory, the pressure exerted by a gas is caused by the bombardment of the gas molecules on the walls of the container.

  • The air molecules in a tyre move rapidly in all directions and collide with the inner walls; these collisions exert the pressure.
  • The pressure is the same at all points on the wall because the molecules are spread evenly and move randomly, so collisions happen equally often everywhere.
  • With twice as many molecules at the same temperature and volume, there are twice as many collisions per second, so the pressure doubles.

Heating and Cooling a Gas

  • If a gas is heated in a sealed cylinder, its temperature, the average kinetic energy of its particles and the pressure inside all increase.
  • A heated gas in a fixed volume: the molecules move faster (they do not expand, and they cannot move further apart in a fixed volume).
  • When a gas is cooled in a sealed tube: the size and number of the molecules do not change; the molecules move more slowly, so the pressure falls; if cooled enough, the gas condenses into a liquid and may then freeze.
  • When a liquid cools down, its molecules slow down and move less freely; on further cooling the liquid freezes into a solid, where the molecules only vibrate in fixed positions.

mcqs.q: According to kinetic molecular theory, the pressure exerted by a gas is caused by the ______.
options: bombardment of the gas molecules on the walls of the container
mcqs.why: Gas pressure comes from the countless collisions of the rapidly moving molecules with the walls of the container — their bombardment of the walls exerts the pressure.

mcqs.q: If a gas is heated in a sealed cylinder, then ______ increases.
options: average kinetic energy of the particles
mcqs.why: Heating raises the temperature, which raises the average kinetic energy of the molecules; they hit the walls harder and more often, so the pressure increases too. All three increase.

mcqs.q: A gas in a container of fixed volume is heated. What happens to the molecules of the gas?
mcqs.why: Heating increases the kinetic energy, so the molecules move faster. The molecules themselves do not expand, and in a fixed volume they cannot move further apart on average.

mcqs.q: A sample of gas in a sealed test tube is cooled. What happens to the size and number of its molecules?
options: Neither changes — the molecules just move more slowly
The size increases, the number stays the same
mcqs.why: Cooling does not change the molecules themselves: their size and number stay the same (the tube is sealed). Only their speed and kinetic energy fall, so the pressure falls.

mcqs.q: When the gas in the sealed tube is cooled, the pressure inside the tube:
options: falls, because the slower molecules collide less energetically with the walls
mcqs.why: Cooler molecules move more slowly and strike the walls less hard and less often, so the pressure inside the sealed tube falls as the gas cools.

mcqs.q: If a cooled gas is cooled still further, it may:
options: turn into a solid directly only
condense into a liquid and may then freeze into a solid
mcqs.why: As cooling continues the molecules come closer together and the gas condenses into a liquid; further cooling can freeze the liquid into a solid.

mcqs.q: How does the air inside a tyre exert pressure on the walls of the tyre?
options: The air molecules move rapidly in all directions and collide with (bombard) the inner walls
mcqs.why: The rapidly moving air molecules collide with the inner walls of the tyre in all directions; the force of these collisions spread over the wall area is the pressure.

mcqs.q: The pressure is the same at all points on the inside wall of the tyre because:
options: the molecules are spread evenly and move randomly, so collisions occur equally often at every point
mcqs.why: Random motion spreads the molecules evenly through the tyre, so every part of the wall receives the same rate of collisions and the pressure is the same everywhere.

mcqs.q: More air is pumped into a tyre at constant temperature until there are twice as many molecules. The pressure is expected to:
options: double, because there are twice as many collisions per second with the walls
mcqs.why: At fixed volume and temperature, pressure is proportional to the number of molecules. Twice as many molecules means twice as many wall collisions per second, so the pressure doubles.

mcqs.q: When a liquid is cooled down, its molecules:
options: slow down and move less freely, and on further cooling the liquid freezes into a solid
mcqs.why: Cooling removes kinetic energy: liquid molecules move more slowly and less freely, and with enough cooling the liquid freezes — its molecules then only vibrate in fixed positions in the solid.

lessons.title: Change of State: Melting, Boiling, Evaporation and Condensation
lessons.notes_html:
Changes of state happen when particles gain or lose energy:

  • Melting — solid changes to liquid at the melting point.
  • Freezing — liquid changes to solid.
  • Boiling — liquid changes to gas at the boiling point, throughout the liquid.
  • Condensing — gas changes into a liquid; the molecules move closer and lose energy.
  • Evaporation — in a liquid, some energetic molecules break free from the surface even when the liquid is too cold for bubbles to form.

Reading Melting and Boiling Points

A substance with melting point −17 °C and boiling point 117 °C is a liquid at any temperature between them — for example at −10 °C and at 110 °C.

mcqs.q: During which process does a gas become a liquid?
mcqs.why: Condensing (condensation) is the change from gas to liquid, when the molecules lose energy and come closer together. Boiling is the opposite change, liquid to gas.

mcqs.q: In a liquid, some energetic molecules break free from the surface even when the liquid is too cold for bubbles to form. This process is called:
mcqs.why: Evaporation is the escape of the most energetic molecules from the surface of a liquid at any temperature, even when the liquid is far below its boiling point.

mcqs.q: What happens to the molecules of a gas when the gas changes into a liquid?
options: They move closer and gain energy
They move closer and lose energy
They move apart and lose energy
They move apart and gain energy
mcqs.why: Condensation: the gas molecules lose energy, slow down and come closer together until they form a liquid. Gaining energy and moving apart describes evaporation or boiling.

mcqs.q: A substance has a melting point of −17 °C and a boiling point of 117 °C. Its state at −10 °C and at 110 °C is:
mcqs.why: Both −10 °C and 110 °C lie between the melting point (−17 °C) and the boiling point (117 °C). Between these two temperatures the substance is a liquid.

mcqs.q: At a temperature below its melting point, a substance exists as:
mcqs.why: Below the melting point the particles do not have enough energy to leave their fixed positions, so the substance is a solid.

mcqs.q: At a temperature above its boiling point, a substance exists as:
mcqs.why: Above the boiling point all the particles have enough energy to move freely and far apart, so the substance exists as a gas.

mcqs.q: When a liquid boils, the change of state happens:
options: throughout the liquid at the boiling point
mcqs.why: Boiling takes place throughout the liquid — bubbles form inside it — and only at the fixed boiling point. Evaporation, in contrast, happens only at the surface and at all temperatures.

mcqs.q: Melting is the change of state from:
mcqs.why: Melting (fusion) changes a solid into a liquid at its melting point. Liquid to solid is freezing, and liquid to gas is boiling or evaporation.

mcqs.q: During condensation, the molecules of the gas:
options: lose energy and come closer together
mcqs.why: To condense, gas molecules must lose energy; they slow down, come closer and are held together as a liquid. This is why condensing steam releases heat.

mcqs.q: Evaporation takes place:
options: only at the surface of a liquid, at any temperature
mcqs.why: Evaporation is a surface process: the fastest molecules escape from the surface of the liquid, and it can happen at any temperature, not just at the boiling point.

lessons.title: Boyle's Law: Pressure and Volume of a Gas
lessons.notes_html:
For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, the pressure and volume are linked by Boyle's law:

P1V1 = P2V2

Doubling the pressure (at fixed temperature) halves the volume.

Worked Example 1

The pressure on 9 cm³ of oxygen gas is doubled at fixed temperature. Find the new volume.

Step 1: By Boyle's law, P1V1 = P2V2

Step 2: Doubling the pressure halves the volume: V2 = 9 cm³ / 2

Step 3: V2 = 4.5 cm³

Worked Example 2

A container holds 30 m³ of air at a pressure of 150 000 Pa. The volume is changed to 10 m³ at constant temperature. Find the new pressure.

Step 1: P2 = P1V1 / V2

Step 2: P2 = 150 000 Pa × 30 m³ / 10 m³

Step 3: P2 = 450 000 Pa

Worked Example 3

Air at 760 mm of Hg is trapped with a movable piston. The volume is increased from 100 dm³ to 150 dm³ at constant temperature. Find the pressure.

Step 1: P2 = P1V1 / V2 = 760 × 100 / 150

Step 2: P2 = 506.7 mm of Hg (about 507 mm Hg)

mcqs.q: Boyle's law, for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, is written as:
mcqs.why: Boyle's law: at constant temperature the product of pressure and volume stays constant, P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>. Pressure and volume are inversely proportional.

mcqs.q: The pressure on 9 cm³ of oxygen gas is doubled at a fixed temperature. Its volume will become:
mcqs.why: Step 1: P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub> with P<sub>2</sub> = 2P<sub>1</sub>. Step 2: V<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>1</sub> / 2 = 9 / 2. Step 3: V<sub>2</sub> = 4.5 cm³. Doubling the pressure halves the volume.

mcqs.q: A container holds 30 m³ of air at 150 000 Pa. The volume is changed to 10 m³ at constant temperature. The new pressure is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: P<sub>2</sub> = P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> / V<sub>2</sub>. Step 2: = 150 000 × 30 / 10. Step 3: P<sub>2</sub> = 450 000 Pa. Shrinking the volume to one-third triples the pressure.

mcqs.q: Air at 760 mm of Hg is expanded from 100 dm³ to 150 dm³ at constant temperature. Its pressure becomes:
mcqs.why: Step 1: P<sub>2</sub> = P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> / V<sub>2</sub> = 760 × 100 / 150. Step 2: P<sub>2</sub> = 506.7 ≈ 507 mm of Hg. A larger volume means a smaller pressure.

mcqs.q: Boyle's law applies when which two things are kept constant?
options: Temperature and the mass of gas
mcqs.why: Boyle's law holds for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature. If the temperature changes, P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub> no longer applies directly.

mcqs.q: If the volume of a gas is halved at constant temperature, its pressure:
mcqs.why: From P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>: halving V means P must double to keep the product constant. Pressure and volume are inversely proportional.

mcqs.q: A gas occupies 20 cm³ at a pressure of 300 kPa. At constant temperature its volume is increased to 60 cm³. The new pressure is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: P<sub>2</sub> = P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> / V<sub>2</sub> = 300 × 20 / 60. Step 2: P<sub>2</sub> = 100 kPa. Tripling the volume divides the pressure by three.

mcqs.q: According to the kinetic theory, Boyle's law works because when a gas is compressed into a smaller volume:
options: the molecules hit the walls more often, raising the pressure
mcqs.why: In a smaller volume the same molecules are crowded closer to the walls and collide with them more frequently, so the pressure rises — the microscopic reason behind Boyle's law.

mcqs.q: The unit mm of Hg measures:
mcqs.why: Millimetres of mercury (mm of Hg) is a pressure unit based on the height of a mercury column; atmospheric pressure is 760 mm of Hg.

mcqs.q: A syringe of air is sealed and the piston is pushed in slowly, keeping the temperature constant. The pressure of the air inside:
options: increases, because the volume has decreased
mcqs.why: Pushing the piston in reduces the volume at constant temperature, so by Boyle's law the pressure must increase in inverse proportion.

chapters.title: Unit 8: Energy Sources and Transfer of Energy

lessons.title: Work
lessons.notes_html:
Work is done when a force moves a body through a distance in the direction of the force:

W = F × d

If the force F acts at an angle θ to the displacement d, only the component of the force along the displacement, F cos θ, does work:

W = Fd cos θ

The SI unit of work is the joule (J).

Worked Example 1

How much work is needed to move a body 20 m horizontally by a force of 30 N applied at 60° to the horizontal?

Step 1: W = Fd cos θ = 30 N × 20 m × cos 60°

Step 2: W = 30 × 20 × 0.5

Step 3: W = 300 J

Worked Example 2

A crate is moved 50 m with a force of 30 N applied along the surface. Work done = F × d = 30 N × 50 m = 1500 J.

Zero Work

If a bar of weight 100 N is carried from A to B and then brought back to A, the net displacement is zero, so the net work done is zero: W = F × 0 = 0 J. Work done in one direction is cancelled on the return.

mcqs.q: If a force of 6 N displaces an object 2 m in the direction of the force, the work done will be ______.
mcqs.why: Step 1: W = F × d. Step 2: W = 6 N × 2 m. Step 3: W = 12 J. Work is measured in joules, not newtons.

mcqs.q: Work is done when:
options: a force moves a body through a distance in the direction of the force
a force acts but nothing moves
a force acts at 90° to the motion only
mcqs.why: Work = force × distance moved in the direction of the force. If there is no displacement, no work is done however large the force.

mcqs.q: The equation for work done by a force acting at an angle θ to the displacement is:
mcqs.why: Only the component of the force along the displacement, F cos θ, does work, so W = (F cos θ) × d = Fd cos θ.

mcqs.q: How much work is needed to move a body 20 m by a force of 30 N at 60° to the horizontal?
mcqs.why: Step 1: W = Fd cos θ = 30 × 20 × cos 60°. Step 2: cos 60° = 0.5, so W = 30 × 20 × 0.5. Step 3: W = 300 J.

mcqs.q: A crate is moved a distance of 50 m by a force of 30 N applied along the surface. The work done is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: The force is along the displacement, so W = F × d. Step 2: W = 30 N × 50 m. Step 3: W = 1500 J.

mcqs.q: A bar is carried from A to B and then brought back to A. The net work done is:
options: zero, because the net displacement is zero
mcqs.why: Work depends on the displacement. The bar ends where it started, so the net displacement is zero and W = F × 0 = 0 J; the outward work is cancelled on the return.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of work is:
mcqs.why: Work = force (N) × distance (m), so its unit is the newton-metre, named the joule (J).

mcqs.q: A force of 50 N moves a body 4 m in its own direction. The work done is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: W = F × d = 50 N × 4 m. Step 2: W = 200 J.

mcqs.q: If the force acts at 90° to the displacement, the work done is:
mcqs.why: W = Fd cos θ with θ = 90° gives W = Fd × 0 = 0. A force perpendicular to the motion does no work (like the centripetal force on a circling body).

mcqs.q: Work done is a ______ quantity.
mcqs.why: Work has magnitude and unit (joule) but no direction of its own, so it is a scalar quantity — even though it is calculated from two vectors, force and displacement.

lessons.title: Kinetic Energy and Potential Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Kinetic energy is the energy a body has because of its motion:

K.E = ½mv²

Derivation: the work done to speed up a mass m from rest to velocity v is W = F × d = ma × d. From v² = 2ad, d = v² / 2a, so W = ma × (v² / 2a) = ½mv². This work is stored as kinetic energy.

Potential energy is the energy stored in a body because of its position or state:

P.E = mgh

Derivation: the work done to lift a mass m through height h against gravity is W = F × d = (mg) × h = mgh, and this work is stored as potential energy.

Worked Examples

Boy on a bike: K.E = ½ × 50 kg × (2 ms&sup-1;)² = ½ × 50 × 4 = 100 J

LED screen lifted onto a cupboard: P.E = mgh = 10 kg × 10 ms&sup-2; × 2 m = 200 J

Water raised to a roof tank: P.E = mgh = 3 kg × 10 ms&sup-2; × 4 m = 120 J

mcqs.q: If a body of mass 1 kg is moving with a velocity of 1 m/s, the K.E of the body will be ______.
mcqs.why: Step 1: K.E = ½mv². Step 2: K.E = ½ × 1 kg × (1 m/s)². Step 3: K.E = 0.5 J.

mcqs.q: A body of mass 1 kg is lifted through a height of 1 m (g = 10 ms&sup-2;). The energy possessed by the body will be ______.
mcqs.why: Step 1: P.E = mgh. Step 2: P.E = 1 kg × 10 ms&sup-2; × 1 m. Step 3: P.E = 10 J. The lifted body stores this as potential energy.

mcqs.q: Kinetic energy is the energy a body has because of its:
mcqs.why: Kinetic energy is energy of motion: K.E = ½mv². A body at rest has no kinetic energy; energy due to position is potential energy.

mcqs.q: The equation for kinetic energy is:
mcqs.why: K.E = ½mv² — half the mass times the square of the velocity. Doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times greater.

mcqs.q: What will be the kinetic energy of a boy of mass 50 kg riding a bike with a velocity of 2 ms&sup-1;?
mcqs.why: Step 1: K.E = ½mv² = ½ × 50 × 2². Step 2: = ½ × 50 × 4. Step 3: K.E = 100 J.

mcqs.q: Potential energy is the energy stored in a body because of its:
mcqs.why: Potential energy is stored energy of position or state — e.g. a lifted mass (mgh) or a stretched spring. It can be released to do work.

mcqs.q: The equation for gravitational potential energy is:
mcqs.why: P.E = mgh: the work done lifting a mass m through height h against gravity g is stored as potential energy.

mcqs.q: An LED screen of mass 10 kg is lifted and kept on a cupboard of height 2 m (g = 10 ms&sup-2;). Its potential energy is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: P.E = mgh = 10 × 10 × 2. Step 2: P.E = 200 J.

mcqs.q: Calculate the potential energy of 3 kg of water raised to a roof tank 4 m high (g = 10 ms&sup-2;).
mcqs.why: Step 1: P.E = mgh = 3 kg × 10 ms&sup-2; × 4 m. Step 2: P.E = 120 J.

mcqs.q: In deriving K.E = ½mv², the relation d = v² / 2a comes from:
options: v² = 2ad for a body starting from rest
mcqs.why: Work = ma × d; using v² = 2ad (starting from rest) gives d = v² / 2a, and substituting gives W = ½mv², which is stored as kinetic energy.

lessons.title: Energy Sources and Energy Conversion
lessons.notes_html:
Energy is converted from one form to another. The book describes the processes by which energy is converted with reference to fossil fuel energy, hydroelectric generation, solar energy, nuclear energy, geothermal energy, wind energy, biomass energy and tidal energy.

Fossil Fuel Energy

Coal, oil and natural gas are fossil fuels. They took millions of years to form from dead plants and animals.

Solar Energy

Solar energy is the energy we get from the Sun's light and heat. Pakistan gets strong sunshine almost all year; solar power can supply electricity, reduce load-shedding, serve remote areas without grid lines, and cut fuel imports and pollution. Devices: a solar water heater (or solar cooker) converts solar energy into heat energy; solar cells and solar panels convert it into electrical energy.

Nuclear Energy

The energy released during a fission or fusion reaction is called nuclear energy. Uranium (Uranium-235) is a radioactive element used as a source of nuclear energy.

Wind Energy

Wind energy (the book prints 'wing energy') is the energy of moving air. Applications: generating electricity with wind turbines; pumping water from wells; grinding grain with windmills; driving sailing ships.

Tidal Energy

Energy from the rise and fall of sea tides, caused by the Moon's (and Sun's) gravitational pull. Tidal barrages and underwater turbines turn this moving water into electricity.

Geothermal Energy

Heat from inside the Earth (hot rocks and magma below the surface). It is used to make electricity (steam turbines) and for direct heating.

mcqs.q: The energy released during a fission or fusion reaction is called ______.
mcqs.why: Fission (splitting heavy nuclei) and fusion (joining light nuclei) release nuclear energy — the energy stored in the nucleus of the atom, e.g. from uranium.

mcqs.q: Coal, gas and oil are all examples of ______.
mcqs.why: Coal, oil and natural gas were formed from dead plants and animals over millions of years, so they are called fossil fuels.

mcqs.q: Solar energy is:
options: energy from the Sun's light and heat
mcqs.why: Solar energy is the energy we receive from the Sun as light and heat. Energy from inside the Earth is geothermal, and from tides is tidal energy.

mcqs.q: A radioactive element used as a source of nuclear energy is:
mcqs.why: Uranium-235 is the radioactive element whose fission in nuclear reactors releases nuclear energy for generating electricity.

mcqs.q: A device that can convert solar energy into heat energy is:
options: a solar water heater (or solar cooker)
mcqs.why: A solar water heater (or solar cooker) absorbs sunlight and turns it into heat. Solar cells and panels convert sunlight into electrical energy instead.

mcqs.q: Two devices that convert solar energy into electrical energy are:
options: solar cooker and solar water heater
mcqs.why: Solar cells and solar (photovoltaic) panels convert sunlight directly into electrical energy. Solar cookers and water heaters produce heat, not electricity.

mcqs.q: Wind energy is:
mcqs.why: Wind energy is the kinetic energy of moving air (the book prints it as 'wing energy'). It drives wind turbines, windmills and sailing ships.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an application of wind energy?
mcqs.why: Wind turbines use moving air to generate electricity. Wind energy is also used to pump water from wells, grind grain in windmills and drive sailing ships.

mcqs.q: Tidal energy comes from:
options: the rise and fall of sea tides, caused by the Moon's (and Sun's) gravitational pull
mcqs.why: Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravitational pull on the oceans. Tidal barrages and underwater turbines convert the moving tidal water into electricity.

mcqs.q: Geothermal energy is:
mcqs.why: Geothermal energy is the heat stored inside the Earth in hot rocks and magma. It is used to generate electricity with steam turbines and for direct heating.

lessons.title: Renewable and Non-renewable Energy Sources
lessons.notes_html:
Renewable Sources

Renewable energy sources are those that nature keeps replacing, so they never run out on human timescales: solar, wind, hydroelectric (flowing water), tidal, geothermal and biomass energy. They are clean and sustainable, and using them reduces pollution and dependence on fossil fuels.

Non-renewable Sources

Non-renewable energy sources exist in limited amounts and are used up much faster than nature can replace them: coal, oil (petroleum), natural gas and nuclear fuel (uranium). Once finished, they cannot be replaced within a human lifetime. Fossil fuels took millions of years to form from dead plants and animals, and we are using them far faster than nature can replace them. Burning fossil fuels also causes air pollution and climate change.

Sorting the Sources

RenewableNon-renewable
Solar, Wind, Tidal, Biomass, HydroelectricityUranium, Coal, Natural gas

mcqs.q: Which is the renewable source of energy?
mcqs.why: Solar and wind energy are continuously replaced by nature, so they are renewable. Coal, natural gas and petroleum are fossil fuels that will run out.

mcqs.q: ______ is not a renewable source of energy.
mcqs.why: Coal is a fossil fuel formed over millions of years and used up far faster than it forms, so it is non-renewable. Solar, wind and geothermal energy are renewable.

mcqs.q: Fossil fuel energy is called non-renewable because fossil fuels:
options: took millions of years to form and are being used far faster than nature can replace them
mcqs.why: Coal, oil and natural gas formed from dead plants and animals over millions of years. Once used up, they cannot be replaced within a human lifetime, so they are non-renewable.

mcqs.q: Which list contains only renewable sources?
mcqs.why: Solar, wind, tidal, biomass and hydroelectricity are all replaced by nature continuously. Uranium, coal and natural gas are finite, non-renewable sources.

mcqs.q: Uranium is classified as:
mcqs.why: Uranium exists in a limited amount in the Earth's crust and is not replaced by nature, so nuclear fuel is a non-renewable source (though it is not a fossil fuel).

mcqs.q: Renewable energy sources are those that:
options: must be burnt to give energy
nature keeps replacing, so they never run out on human timescales
mcqs.why: Renewable sources — solar, wind, hydro, tidal, geothermal, biomass — are replenished by nature as fast as we use them, so they do not run out on human timescales.

mcqs.q: Non-renewable energy sources are those that:
options: exist in limited amounts and are used up faster than nature can replace them
mcqs.why: Coal, oil, natural gas and uranium are finite: once the deposits are used up they are gone for human purposes, because nature replaces them extremely slowly or not at all.

mcqs.q: An advantage of renewable sources over fossil fuels is that they:
options: are clean and sustainable and reduce dependence on fossil fuels
mcqs.why: Renewable sources are clean and sustainable; using them reduces air pollution and climate change and cuts dependence on imported fossil fuels.

mcqs.q: Hydroelectric energy (from flowing water) is:
mcqs.why: Flowing water is part of the natural water cycle, which keeps renewing it, so hydroelectricity is a renewable source of energy.

mcqs.q: Burning fossil fuels causes:
mcqs.why: Burning coal, oil and gas releases smoke and carbon dioxide, causing air pollution and climate change — a major reason to shift to renewable sources.

lessons.title: Efficiency
lessons.notes_html:
Efficiency is the ratio of the useful output of a machine to its total input, given as a percentage:

Efficiency = (output / input) × 100

Efficiency is always less than 100% because some input energy is always lost as heat, sound or friction. That is why a system cannot have an efficiency of 100%.

Worked Example 1

A machine consumes 200 J of energy and performs 50 J of work. Efficiency = (50 / 200) × 100 = 25%.

Worked Example 2

The efficiency of a machine is 70% and its output is 100 J. Find its input.

Step 1: Input = output / efficiency

Step 2: Input = 100 J / 0.70 = 142.9 J (about 143 J)

Worked Example 3

Machine A: output 200 J after consuming 400 J. Machine B: output 300 J after consuming 450 J. Which is more efficient?

Step 1: A: 200 / 400 × 100 = 50%

Step 2: B: 300 / 450 × 100 = 66.7%

Step 3: Machine B is more efficient.

mcqs.q: The ratio of output to input is called ______.
mcqs.why: Efficiency = output / input (usually × 100 as a percentage). It compares the useful energy a machine gives out with the total energy put into it.

mcqs.q: Calculate the efficiency of a machine which consumes 200 J of energy and performs 50 J of work.
mcqs.why: Step 1: Efficiency = (output / input) × 100. Step 2: = (50 / 200) × 100. Step 3: Efficiency = 25%.

mcqs.q: If the efficiency of a machine is 70% and its output is 100 J, its input is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Input = output / efficiency = 100 / 0.70. Step 2: Input = 142.9 J ≈ 143 J. The input is always larger than the output.

mcqs.q: Machine A gives 200 J output from 400 J input; machine B gives 300 J output from 450 J input. Which is more efficient?
mcqs.why: Step 1: A = 200 / 400 × 100 = 50%. Step 2: B = 300 / 450 × 100 = 66.7%. Step 3: Machine B converts a bigger share of its input into useful output, so B is more efficient.

mcqs.q: Efficiency of a machine is always less than 100% because:
options: some input energy is always lost as heat, sound or friction
mcqs.why: No machine converts all its input into useful work; some energy is always wasted as heat, sound and friction, so efficiency is always below 100%.

mcqs.q: The efficiency formula is:
mcqs.why: Efficiency = (energy converted into the required form / total energy input) × 100, expressed as a percentage with no unit.

mcqs.q: A machine with input 500 J and efficiency 60% gives a useful output of:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Output = efficiency × input = 0.60 × 500 J. Step 2: Output = 300 J. The remaining 200 J is wasted as heat, sound or friction.

mcqs.q: Why can a system not have an efficiency of 100%?
options: Because output is always greater than input
Because some energy is always wasted as heat, sound or friction
mcqs.why: Friction and other losses are unavoidable in any real system, so a part of the input is always wasted and efficiency can never reach 100%.

mcqs.q: Efficiency is expressed as:
mcqs.why: Efficiency is a ratio of two energies, so the units cancel; it is written as a percentage and has no unit of its own.

mcqs.q: A bulb takes 100 J of electrical energy and gives 10 J of light. Its efficiency is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Efficiency = (output / input) × 100 = (10 / 100) × 100. Step 2: Efficiency = 10%. The other 90 J is wasted as heat.

lessons.title: Power
lessons.notes_html:
Power is the rate of doing work (or of transferring energy):

P = W / t

The SI unit of power is the watt (W): 1 watt = 1 joule per second (1 W = 1 J/s). Larger units of power include the kilowatt (kW) and megawatt (MW); horsepower (hp) is also used, with 1 hp = 746 W.

Worked Example 1

The energy of 600 J is dissipated by a bulb in 50 minutes. Find the power of the bulb.

Step 1: Time = 50 × 60 = 3000 s

Step 2: P = W / t = 600 J / 3000 s = 0.2 W

Worked Example 2

A student of weight 400 N takes 5 s to climb an obstacle of height 2 m. Find the power.

Step 1: Work = F × h = 400 N × 2 m = 800 J

Step 2: P = W / t = 800 J / 5 s = 160 W

More Examples

  • Convert 20 W into horsepower: 20 / 746 = 0.0268 hp
  • A machine doing 40 J of work in 10 s has power P = 40 / 10 = 4 W
  • A machine consuming 250 J per hour has power P = 250 / 3600 = 0.0694 W (about 0.07 W)

mcqs.q: If a machine performs 20 J of work in 10 s, its power is ______.
mcqs.why: Step 1: P = W / t. Step 2: P = 20 J / 10 s. Step 3: P = 2 W.

mcqs.q: Work done per unit time is called ______.
mcqs.why: Power is the rate of doing work: P = W / t. Efficiency is a ratio of energies, and force is a push or pull — neither is a rate.

mcqs.q: Power is defined as:
options: the rate of doing work, P = W / t
mcqs.why: Power measures how fast work is done or energy is transferred: P = W / t, measured in watts.

mcqs.q: The energy of 600 J is dissipated by a bulb in 50 minutes. The power of the bulb is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: t = 50 × 60 = 3000 s. Step 2: P = W / t = 600 J / 3000 s. Step 3: P = 0.2 W (the book's worked example).

mcqs.q: Define the watt.
options: 1 watt = 1 joule per second (1 W = 1 J/s)
mcqs.why: The watt is the SI unit of power: a power of 1 watt means work is done (or energy transferred) at the rate of 1 joule per second.

mcqs.q: A student of weight 400 N climbs a height of 2 m in 5 s. The power consumed is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: Work = F × h = 400 × 2 = 800 J. Step 2: P = W / t = 800 / 5. Step 3: P = 160 W.

mcqs.q: Convert 20 watt into horsepower (1 hp = 746 W).
mcqs.why: Step 1: hp = W / 746. Step 2: 20 / 746 = 0.0268 hp. Horsepower is a larger unit than the watt, so the number becomes smaller.

mcqs.q: A machine does 40 Joules of work in 10 sec. Its power is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: P = W / t = 40 J / 10 s. Step 2: P = 4 W.

mcqs.q: Two larger units of power are:
mcqs.why: For large powers we use the kilowatt (1 kW = 1000 W) and the megawatt (1 MW = 1 000 000 W). Horsepower is another larger unit used for engines.

mcqs.q: A machine consumes 250 J of energy per hour. Its power is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: t = 1 hour = 3600 s. Step 2: P = E / t = 250 J / 3600 s. Step 3: P = 0.0694 W ≈ 0.07 W.

lessons.title: Temperature, Heat and Thermal Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Temperature

Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body. It is measured with a thermometer. Its SI unit is the kelvin (K).

Temperature Scales

Three scales are used: Celsius (°C), Fahrenheit (°F) and kelvin (K). The conversion formulas are:

K = °C + 273

°F = 1.8 × °C + 32

°C = (°F − 32) / 1.8

PointCelsiusFahrenheitKelvin
Melting point of ice0 °C32 °F273 K
Boiling point of water100 °C212 °F373 K
Absolute zero−273 °C−459 °F0 K

Worked Example: Converting 25 °C

Step 1: To kelvin: K = °C + 273 = 25 + 273 = 298 K

Step 2: To Fahrenheit: °F = 1.8 × °C + 32 = 1.8 × 25 + 32

Step 3: °F = 45 + 32 = 77 °F

Thermal Energy and Internal Energy

  • Thermal energy is the total kinetic energy of all the particles of a body.
  • Internal energy of a system is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of all the particles of the system.
  • A bigger body, or a hotter body, has more internal energy because it has more particle energy in total.

Heat

  • Heat is thermal energy in transfer: it flows from a hotter body to a colder one because of the temperature difference between them.
  • Heat is measured in joules (J).
  • Heat keeps flowing until both bodies reach the same temperature.
  • Heat is not stored in a body; what is stored is internal (thermal) energy. Heat is the name of the energy while it is being transferred.

mcqs.q: The internal energy of a system is the sum of:
options: the kinetic energy of the body as a whole
the kinetic and potential energies of all its particles
mcqs.why: Internal energy is the total energy stored in the particles of a system: the kinetic energies of their motion plus the potential energies of their positions. The book's own answer states this: internal energy is the total of the kinetic and potential energies of all the particles.

mcqs.q: Heat is best defined as:
options: thermal energy transferred from a hotter body to a colder body because of a temperature difference
the total energy stored in a body
the kinetic energy of the particles of a body
mcqs.why: Heat is thermal energy in transfer. It exists only while energy is moving from a hotter body to a colder one because of their temperature difference; the energy stored inside a body is called thermal (internal) energy, not heat.

mcqs.q: The thermal energy of a body is:
options: the heat flowing out of the body
the total kinetic energy of all the particles of the body
the potential energy of the body due to its height
the temperature of the body in kelvin
mcqs.why: Thermal energy is defined as the total kinetic energy of all the particles of a body. Every particle is moving, and thermal energy adds up the kinetic energy of every one of them.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of temperature is the:
mcqs.why: The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of temperature. Celsius and Fahrenheit are common practical scales, and the joule is the unit of energy and heat, not of temperature.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of heat is the:
mcqs.why: Heat is a form of energy, so it is measured in joules (J), the SI unit of energy. The watt is the unit of power and the kelvin is the unit of temperature.

mcqs.q: 0 °C expressed in kelvin is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: K = °C + 273. Step 2: K = 0 + 273. Step 3: K = 273 K. So the melting point of ice, 0 °C, is 273 K.

mcqs.q: The boiling point of water (100 °C) on the Fahrenheit scale is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: °F = 1.8 × °C + 32. Step 2: °F = 1.8 × 100 + 32 = 180 + 32. Step 3: °F = 212 °F.

mcqs.q: Convert 30 °C to the Fahrenheit scale:
mcqs.why: Step 1: °F = 1.8 × °C + 32. Step 2: °F = 1.8 × 30 + 32 = 54 + 32. Step 3: °F = 86 °F.

mcqs.q: Convert 300 K to the Celsius scale:
mcqs.why: Step 1: °C = K − 273. Step 2: °C = 300 − 273. Step 3: °C = 27 °C.

mcqs.q: When a hot body and a cold body are placed in contact, heat flows:
options: from the hotter body to the colder body until both reach the same temperature
from the colder body to the hotter body
in both directions equally from the start
only if the hotter body is bigger
mcqs.why: Heat is thermal energy in transfer, and it always flows from the hotter body to the colder one because of the temperature difference. The flow stops when both bodies reach the same temperature.

lessons.title: Heat Capacity and Specific Heat Capacity
lessons.notes_html:
Heat Capacity

The heat capacity of a body is the heat needed to raise the temperature of the whole body by 1 °C:

C = Q / ΔT

Its unit is J per degree C (J/°C), or J/K.

Specific Heat Capacity

The specific heat capacity of a substance is the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 °C:

c = Q / (m ΔT)

Its unit is J kg−1 °C−1. Rearranging gives the heat equation:

Q = m c ΔT

So the heat needed depends on three things: the mass m, the specific heat capacity c of the material, and the temperature change ΔT.

The specific heat capacity of water is very high:

c (water) = 4200 J kg−1 °C−1

Worked Example 1 (Book)

One litre of water (mass 1 kg) is heated by 4 °C. How much heat is supplied? (c = 4200 J kg−1 °C−1)

Step 1: Q = m c ΔT

Step 2: Q = 1 kg × 4200 J kg−1 °C−1 × 4 °C

Step 3: Q = 16 800 J

Worked Example 2 (Book)

Heat is supplied to 2 kg of ice and its temperature rises by 15 °C. How much heat is absorbed? (c of ice = 1000 J kg−1 °C−1)

Step 1: Q = m c ΔT

Step 2: Q = 2 kg × 1000 J kg−1 °C−1 × 15 °C

Step 3: Q = 30 000 J

Worked Example 3 (Book)

Find the heat absorbed by a 5 kg metal when its temperature rises from 20 °C to 80 °C. (c = 0.39 kJ kg−1 °C−1)

Step 1: ΔT = 80 °C − 20 °C = 60 °C

Step 2: Q = m c ΔT = 5 kg × 0.39 kJ kg−1 °C−1 × 60 °C

Step 3: Q = 117 kJ

Worked Example 4 (Book)

1.5 kg of metal is heated from 10 °C to 60 °C and absorbs 5000 J of heat. Find its specific heat capacity.

Step 1: ΔT = 60 °C − 10 °C = 50 °C

Step 2: c = Q / (m ΔT) = 5000 J / (1.5 kg × 50 °C)

Step 3: c = 5000 / 75 = 66.7 J kg−1 °C−1

Worked Example 5 (Book)

A 0.5 kg substance is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C and absorbs 12 500 J. Find its specific heat capacity.

Step 1: ΔT = 70 °C − 20 °C = 50 °C

Step 2: c = Q / (m ΔT) = 12 500 J / (0.5 kg × 50 °C)

Step 3: c = 12 500 / 25 = 500 J kg−1 °C−1

Worked Example 6 (Book)

900 J of energy raises the temperature of a 2.5 kg block of metal by 20 °C. (a) Heat capacity: C = Q / ΔT = 900 J / 20 °C = 45 J/°C. (b) Specific heat capacity: c = C / m = 45 J/°C / 2.5 kg = 18 J kg−1 °C−1.

Note: 18 J kg−1 °C−1 is far below the specific heat of any real metal (real metals are in the hundreds); the value is kept exactly as the book's numbers give it.

Two Book Values to Note

The book also asks for the specific heat of a 5 kg metal raised by 25 °C with 500 J: c = 500 / (5 × 25) = 4 J kg−1 °C−1. This is far below any real metal, so a misprint in the book's numbers is suspected; the calculation itself is shown as printed.

In another question the book gives the specific heat of water, 4200 J kg−1 °C−1, for a 200 g piece of metal heated through 5 °C: Q = 0.2 kg × 4200 × 5 = 4200 J. The value is used exactly as given in the book.

mcqs.q: The amount of heat energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C is called its:
mcqs.why: Specific heat capacity c is the heat needed for 1 kg through 1 °C: c = Q / (m ΔT). Thermal (heat) capacity is for the whole body, and latent heats belong to change of state, where the temperature does not change at all.

mcqs.q: According to Q = m c ΔT, the heat needed to raise the temperature of an object by 1 °C depends on:
options: only the shape of the object
only the temperature of the object
the mass of the object and the specific heat capacity of its material
mcqs.why: Q = m c ΔT shows the heat depends on the mass m and on the specific heat capacity c of the material (for a fixed ΔT). The book's printed key names specific heat only, but its own note adds that it also depends on the mass.

mcqs.q: The unit of specific heat capacity is:
mcqs.why: From c = Q / (m ΔT): joules divided by (kilograms × degrees Celsius) gives J kg<sup>−1</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup>. Plain J/°C is the unit of heat capacity of a whole body.

mcqs.q: The heat capacity of a body is the heat needed to raise:
options: the body to its boiling point
mcqs.why: Heat capacity C = Q / ΔT refers to the whole body: it is the heat that raises the temperature of the entire body by 1 °C, and its unit is J/°C. The per-kilogram quantity is the specific heat capacity.

mcqs.q: The specific heat capacity of water is:
mcqs.why: The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg<sup>−1</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup> — one of the highest of common substances, which is why water heats up and cools down slowly.

mcqs.q: How much heat is needed to raise 1 kg of water by 4 °C? (c = 4200 J kg<sup>−1</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup>)
mcqs.why: Step 1: Q = m c ΔT. Step 2: Q = 1 kg × 4200 J kg<sup>−1</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup> × 4 °C. Step 3: Q = 16 800 J.

mcqs.q: Heat supplied to 2 kg of ice raises its temperature by 15 °C. How much heat is absorbed? (c of ice = 1000 J kg<sup>−1</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup>)
mcqs.why: Step 1: Q = m c ΔT. Step 2: Q = 2 kg × 1000 J kg<sup>−1</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup> × 15 °C. Step 3: Q = 30 000 J.

mcqs.q: A 5 kg metal is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C. The heat absorbed is: (c = 0.39 kJ kg<sup>−1</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup>)
mcqs.why: Step 1: ΔT = 80 − 20 = 60 °C. Step 2: Q = m c ΔT = 5 × 0.39 × 60. Step 3: Q = 117 kJ.

mcqs.q: 1.5 kg of metal heated from 10 °C to 60 °C absorbs 5000 J. Its specific heat capacity is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: ΔT = 60 − 10 = 50 °C. Step 2: c = Q / (m ΔT) = 5000 / (1.5 × 50) = 5000 / 75. Step 3: c = 66.7 J kg<sup>−1</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup>.

mcqs.q: A 0.5 kg substance heated from 20 °C to 70 °C absorbs 12 500 J. Its specific heat capacity is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: ΔT = 70 − 20 = 50 °C. Step 2: c = Q / (m ΔT) = 12 500 / (0.5 × 50) = 12 500 / 25. Step 3: c = 500 J kg<sup>−1</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup>.

lessons.title: Latent Heat and Change of State
lessons.notes_html:
Change of State

  • A substance changes state when it melts, freezes, boils or condenses.
  • During a change of state the temperature stays constant, even though heat is being absorbed or released: the heat changes the arrangement of the particles, not their average kinetic energy.
  • The melting point is the temperature at which a solid changes into a liquid; for ice it is 0 °C.
  • The boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid starts to change into a gas; for water it is 100 °C.

Latent Heat

Latent heat is the heat absorbed or released when a substance changes its state without any change in temperature. For a mass m:

Q = m L

  • Heat of fusion is the heat needed to change 1 kg of a solid into liquid at its melting point without changing its temperature. The latent heat of fusion is this heat per kilogram.
  • Heat of vaporization is the heat needed to change 1 kg of a liquid into gas at its boiling point without changing its temperature. The latent heat of vaporization is this heat per kilogram.
  • For water: L (vaporization) = 2260 kJ kg−1.

Worked Example 1 (Book)

How much heat is needed to convert 1 kg of water into steam at its boiling point?

Step 1: Q = m L

Step 2: Q = 1 kg × 2260 kJ kg−1

Step 3: Q = 2260 kJ

Worked Example 2 (Book)

How much heat is needed to convert 5 kg of water into steam at its boiling point?

Step 1: Q = m L

Step 2: Q = 5 kg × 2260 kJ kg−1

Step 3: Q = 11 300 kJ

mcqs.q: The heat absorbed by a substance in changing state from solid to liquid without change in temperature is called:
mcqs.why: Melting (fusion) at constant temperature uses the latent heat of fusion. Vaporization is liquid to gas, while specific heat capacity and heat capacity describe temperature rises, not changes of state.

mcqs.q: The heat absorbed by a substance in changing state from liquid to gas without change in temperature is called:
mcqs.why: Liquid to gas at constant temperature uses the latent heat of vaporization. Fusion is solid to liquid, and the two heat capacities belong to temperature change, where no change of state happens.

mcqs.q: The heat energy needed to change a liquid into gas without changing its temperature is called:
mcqs.why: The heat of vaporization is the heat that changes a liquid into a gas at the boiling point while the temperature stays fixed. Heat of fusion belongs to melting, a solid changing into a liquid.

mcqs.q: The temperature at which a liquid starts to change into gas is called its:
mcqs.why: The boiling point is the fixed temperature at which a liquid changes into a gas throughout the liquid — for water, 100 °C. Melting and freezing points belong to the solid–liquid change.

mcqs.q: The melting point of ice is:
mcqs.why: Ice melts at 0 °C (273 K). 100 °C is the boiling point of water, and −273 °C is absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature.

mcqs.q: The formula for the heat involved in a change of state is:
mcqs.why: For a change of state, Q = m L, where m is the mass and L is the latent heat per kilogram. Q = m c ΔT is used only when the temperature changes, and during a change of state ΔT = 0.

mcqs.q: How much heat is needed to convert 1 kg of water into steam at its boiling point? (L = 2260 kJ kg<sup>−1</sup>)
mcqs.why: Step 1: Q = m L. Step 2: Q = 1 kg × 2260 kJ kg<sup>−1</sup>. Step 3: Q = 2260 kJ. This is the book's own value for the latent heat of vaporization of water.

mcqs.q: How much heat is needed to convert 5 kg of water into steam at its boiling point? (L = 2260 kJ kg<sup>−1</sup>)
mcqs.why: Step 1: Q = m L. Step 2: Q = 5 kg × 2260 kJ kg<sup>−1</sup>. Step 3: Q = 11 300 kJ — five times the heat needed for 1 kg, as the formula shows.

mcqs.q: While ice is melting at 0 °C, the heat supplied:
options: raises the temperature of the ice
is lost to the surroundings completely
is used to change the state, so the temperature stays at 0 °C
mcqs.why: During a change of state the temperature does not change. The absorbed heat is latent heat: it works against the forces holding the particles in the solid arrangement instead of raising their average kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: The heat of fusion of a substance is the heat needed to change:
options: 1 kg of solid into liquid at its melting point without changing its temperature
1 kg of liquid into gas at its boiling point
