mcqs.why: Heat of fusion is defined for 1 kg of a solid changing into liquid at its melting point, with no temperature change. The liquid-to-gas quantity is the heat of vaporization, and the 1 °C quantities are the heat capacities.

lessons.title: Evaporation and Boiling
lessons.notes_html:
Evaporation

Evaporation is the escape of molecules from the surface of a liquid at any temperature.

  • It happens at all temperatures, but only at the surface of the liquid, and it is a slow process.
  • The fastest-moving surface molecules escape, so the average kinetic energy of the molecules left behind falls — evaporation produces cooling.

Boiling

Boiling is the rapid change of a liquid into gas throughout the liquid, at a fixed temperature — the boiling point.

Evaporation vs Boiling

EvaporationBoiling
Takes place at all temperaturesTakes place only at the boiling point
Occurs only at the surface of the liquidOccurs throughout the liquid
Slow processFast (rapid) process

Vaporization is the general name for liquid changing into gas; it includes evaporation (at all temperatures) and boiling (only at the boiling point).

Factors That Increase the Rate of Evaporation

  • Larger surface area — more molecules are at the surface to escape.
  • Higher temperature — more molecules have enough energy to escape.
  • Higher wind speed — escaped molecules are carried away before they can return.
  • Lower humidity — drier air can accept more vapour; increasing humidity slows evaporation.
  • Lower atmospheric pressure — molecules escape more easily, so decreasing the pressure increases the rate of evaporation.

mcqs.q: Vaporization takes place:
mcqs.why: Vaporization includes evaporation, which happens at all temperatures from the surface of a liquid. Boiling is the special case that happens only at the boiling point, throughout the liquid.

mcqs.q: The rate of evaporation is increased by:
mcqs.why: Lower atmospheric pressure lets surface molecules escape more easily, so evaporation speeds up. Higher humidity, lower temperature and a higher boiling point all slow evaporation down, as the book's answer explains.

mcqs.q: The factors which increase the rate of evaporation are:
mcqs.why: All three factors help molecules leave the surface: a larger surface area exposes more molecules, a higher temperature gives more of them enough energy to escape, and wind carries the escaped molecules away.

mcqs.q: Evaporation takes place:
options: only at the surface of the liquid
only in the middle of the liquid
only at the bottom of the liquid
mcqs.why: Only molecules at the surface can escape into the air, so evaporation is a surface process. Boiling, by contrast, takes place throughout the liquid, with bubbles forming inside it.

mcqs.q: Boiling takes place:
options: throughout the liquid at the fixed boiling point
mcqs.why: Boiling is the rapid change of a liquid into gas throughout the liquid, and it happens only at one fixed temperature — the boiling point of that liquid (100 °C for water).

mcqs.q: Which of the following slows down evaporation?
options: spreading the liquid over a larger area
increasing the humidity of the air
mcqs.why: When the air is already humid, it holds a lot of water vapour, so fewer molecules can escape into it and evaporation slows. Larger area, wind and higher temperature all increase the rate of evaporation.

mcqs.q: Evaporation causes cooling because:
options: the liquid absorbs heat from the air
the temperature of the liquid rises
the fastest-moving molecules escape, lowering the average kinetic energy of those left behind
mcqs.why: The molecules that escape are the ones with the most kinetic energy. Those left behind have a lower average kinetic energy, and temperature follows average kinetic energy, so the liquid cools down.

mcqs.q: Wet clothes dry faster on a windy day because wind:
options: carries away the escaped water molecules, so more can evaporate
lowers the temperature of the clothes
increases the humidity near the clothes
decreases the surface area of the water
mcqs.why: Wind removes the vapour gathered just above the wet surface. With the escaped molecules carried away, more surface molecules can leave, so the rate of evaporation — and the drying — increases.

mcqs.q: A liquid evaporates faster when it is spread out in a wide tray than in a narrow bottle because:
options: a larger surface area lets more molecules escape
mcqs.why: Evaporation happens only at the surface. Spreading the liquid increases the surface area, so more molecules are at the surface and able to escape at any moment.

mcqs.q: Boiling differs from evaporation in that boiling:
options: happens only at the boiling point and throughout the liquid
mcqs.why: The book's comparison: evaporation happens at all temperatures, only at the surface, and is slow; boiling happens only at the boiling point, throughout the liquid, and is fast.

lessons.title: Thermal Expansion
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Thermal Expansion?

Thermal expansion is the increase in the size — length, area or volume — of a body when it is heated.

Expansion of a Solid on Heating

  • The particles of a solid vibrate about fixed positions.
  • On heating, the particles gain energy and vibrate more vigorously.
  • The stronger vibrations push the particles further apart from each other.
  • With the particles further apart, the solid expands in length, area and volume.
  • On cooling, the vibrations weaken and the solid contracts back.

The Anomalous Expansion of Water

  • Almost every substance expands steadily on heating — water does not, between 0 °C and 4 °C.
  • Water contracts when heated from 0 °C to 4 °C, and expands when heated above 4 °C.
  • So the volume of water is smallest, and its density greatest, at 4 °C.
  • Because of this anomaly, ice floats on water.
  • Lakes and ponds freeze from the top down: the ice layer stays on top, and the water below — near 4 °C at the bottom — does not freeze, so aquatic life survives under the ice.

mcqs.q: Thermal expansion is:
options: the decrease in size of a body on heating
the melting of a body on heating
the change of state of a body on heating
the increase in size of a body when it is heated
mcqs.why: Thermal expansion is the increase in the size (length, area or volume) of a body when it is heated. A decrease in size on cooling is contraction, and melting is a change of state, not expansion.

mcqs.q: When a solid is heated, it expands because its particles:
options: vibrate more vigorously and push each other further apart
mcqs.why: On heating, the particles of a solid vibrate more vigorously about their positions and push each other further apart. The larger separations add up over the whole solid, so its length, area and volume all increase.

mcqs.q: Thermal expansion of a body can be an increase in its:
mcqs.why: The book's definition covers all three: heating increases the size of a body, which may be measured as an increase in length, in area or in volume depending on the body and how it is used.

mcqs.q: On cooling, a solid:
options: contracts as its particles vibrate less and come closer together
keeps the same size at all temperatures
mcqs.why: Cooling removes energy, so the particles vibrate less vigorously and settle closer together — the reverse of expansion. This cooling contraction is why expansion on heating must be allowed for in structures.

mcqs.q: Water heated from 0 °C to 4 °C:
mcqs.why: This is the anomalous expansion of water: between 0 °C and 4 °C water contracts on heating, the opposite of normal behaviour. Only above 4 °C does it expand on heating like other liquids.

mcqs.q: The density of water is greatest at:
mcqs.why: Water contracts as it is heated from 0 °C to 4 °C, so its volume is smallest at 4 °C. Smallest volume for the same mass means the greatest density, at 4 °C.

mcqs.q: Above 4 °C, water on heating:
mcqs.why: The anomaly lasts only from 0 °C to 4 °C. Above 4 °C water behaves normally and expands when heated, like other substances.

mcqs.q: Ice floats on water because of:
options: the high specific heat of water
mcqs.why: The book gives this as a direct result of the anomalous expansion of water: because of water's unusual behaviour near 0–4 °C, ice is less dense than the water below it and floats on it.

mcqs.q: In winter, a lake freezes:
mcqs.why: Because of the anomalous expansion of water, the coldest water and the ice stay at the top. The lake therefore freezes from the top down, and the water beneath the ice remains unfrozen.

mcqs.q: Aquatic life can survive in a frozen lake because:
options: the water below the surface ice does not freeze, staying near 4 °C at the bottom
mcqs.why: Densest water (at 4 °C) sinks to the bottom and does not freeze, while only the surface turns to ice. Fish and other aquatic life survive in this unfrozen water below the ice layer.
